#930. Why Scottish football is struggling to produce young talent

Calum Ferguson was an Inverness Caley Thistle academy player but only played twice for the first team

Calum Ferguson achieved what thousands of young footballers dream of when he played for his boyhood club, Inverness Caledonian Thistle, in the Scottish Premiership.

Yet the 31-year-old looks back on his career as proof of a difficult truth about youth development in Scotland.

Ferguson graduated from Caley Thistle's academy at 18 but played just two games for the first team before moving to lower league clubs and then to Canada and New Zealand to try to get top-flight football.

Now a development officer with Alba Football Alliance, he believes Scottish football continues to sell young players and their families the promise of a pathway from the academies to the first team, which for most will never be a reality.

"Parents believe their boy, or their girl, will get to the first team - that they will be a star in football," he told BBC Scotland's Eorpa programme.

"You just fall away from the game and your life changes overnight."

Calum now works as a development officer trying to bring through new talent

His comments come as Scottish football wrestles with a growing concern over the number of homegrown players who are making it to the top of the game.

In September, all 42 SPFL clubs gathered in St Andrews for a summit to discuss why so few young Scottish players are making the grade at elite level.

Data presented to the clubs showed that Scottish players under the age of 21 made up just 4.1% of minutes played in the Scottish Premiership.

By comparison, in the Danish Superliga, a league of the same size, the figure was 15.1%.

In the first round of fixtures in the Scottish Premiership this season, 28% of the starters were born in Scotland.

A stark contrast to similar sized Norway, where homegrown players made up 72% of the starting 11s on their opening weekend.

Nicklas Fuglestad regularly plays for Viking FK in Norway

This is because Norway has strict quotas.

Its league rules state that a club's full squad must include 16 homegrown players and a matchday squad can have a maximum of nine foreign players.

Nicklas Fuglestad is 20, and regularly plays for Viking FK, based in the Norwegian city of Stavanger. He believes quotas are good for the game.

"Everyone I know is very happy with how the Norwegian football league operates," he says.

"It makes it a bit easier for a young player to move up from the academy and make the step into A-league football."

Viking turned their focus to developing academy talent nearly a decade ago, after they were relegated to the second division.

After finishing champions last year, they have made it to the league stage of the Champions League, where they recently started eight Norwegians in their line-up, four of whom had been in their academy.

Another three from their academy came off the bench.

With both Viking FK and BodÃ¸/Glimt in Europe's top competition this year, it could be said that Norway is going through a golden generation.

Their national team reached the World Cup quarter final â and that wasn't just down to man mountain Erling Haaland.

Hakon Grottland says there is more to Norway's recent success than quotas

However, there's more to Norway's success than quotas, according to HÃ¥kon GrÃ¸ttland, head of player development at the Norwegian Football Federation.

He says two big changes over the past 25 years have made a huge difference - the increase in the use of artificial pitches, and more resources being put into coaching and talent development.

GrÃ¸ttland says artificial pitches allowed football to develop from a summer game to a year-round sport, turning Norway into a proper football nation.

Between 2016 and 2025 alone, 539 such pitches were built, with another 586 redeveloped.

Nearly all are open and free to use, so long as official games aren't taking place.

With Scottish football facing a talent crisis, Calum Maclennan examines the SFAâs youth development plans and discovers what Norwayâs successful system can teach Scotland.

GrÃ¸ttland says changes to player development have provided the second boost to the country's game.

"In the period 2010 to 2020 we used a lot of resources, hired a lot of talent coaches, and built some talent systems in Norway, where I think it's quite unique because it's a system that link grassroots football and top club football together," he says.

That talent system is Landslagskollen - or the National Team School (NTS) - that was established in 2013, following the country's failure to qualify for Euro 2012.

It's neither an academy nor a centralised school, but a national development structure connecting grassroots clubs, districts, top clubs and the federation.

Eleven of the 15 players who played in Norway's 2-1 win over Brazil in the round of 16 at this year's World Cup were part of the NTS pathway from under-15 or under-16s.

Despite a disappointing group campaign, a return to the World Cup after decades in the desert was a significant achievement for the Scotland national team.

The question now is whether the next generation can be developed.

The Tartan Army will not want to wait another 28 years.

Erling Haaland helped Norway to victory over Brazil in the World Cup this summer

At the meeting in St Andrews in September, the Scottish FA proposed quotas, as well as financial incentives, in an attempt to increase game time for young Scottish players.

The governing body put forward three suggestions:

Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players to start in all Scottish Cup matches

Two under-21 Scotland-eligible players to start in all Premier Sports Cup matches

Clubs should field Scotland-eligible Under-21 players for an average of 60 minutes in each league game across all four SPFL divisions (6% of available minutes).

Two votes were to take place on the proposals.

The first, on the issue of Scottish Cup rule adoption, should have happened in October at the SFA's AGM, but did not take place.

The SFA now says it is expected to happen in mid-December.

The second vote is due to take place at the SPFL's annual meeting this month.

Adoption of the league and premier sports cup recommendations require 11 out of 12 top flight clubs to vote in favour â a high bar.

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish said he wanted to give young players opportunities

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish told the BBC he did not believe the proposals went far enough â although he said he didn't think they would get voted through if they were more extreme.

"It's probably a little bit unfortunate, the governance in this country, that we can't just be told by one power, look this is what's happening," the 36-year-old said.

The young manager came into his role on an interim basis in March, before landing a permanent contract in the summer.

By the time BBC EÃ²rpa interviewed him in September, he'd given out six debuts to homegrown players.

Having worked in academy football for years, he says he could not sit where he is now and not give youngsters opportunities if they are ready.

A common argument against playing young players is the jeopardy that comes with managing in the Scottish Premiership.

Managers don't want to risk untried young players when they know that a handful of defeats could cost them their job.

"Yeah, you've got a longer term contract but you know that can be short-lived," Craig says.

"It's results based and I'm totally fine with that. I don't fear the negative outcome that can come.

Andrew Robertson and John McGinn both began their careers in the Scottish youth system

In recent years, top players such as Andrew Robertson, John McGinn, and Ryan Christie, have all had a significant grounding in the Scottish Premiership before moving on to greater things.

And regardless of talent coaches or quotas for homegrown players, the Scottish top flight can be extremely entertaining.

That much was clear last season, when fans were treated to the most enticing title race in years.

It is now up to the clubs to decide whether they want their league to be more Scottish.

All will become clear once the votes on the SFA's proposals take place.

Although the delay would suggest things are not going as the governing body would have liked.

#929. Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

#928. Peck hat-trick steers Sheff Utd past Preston

Preston North End vs Sheffield United. Sky Bet Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Preston North End and Sheffield United at Deepdale on Tuesday night; Sydie Peck scores a first career hat-trick in Blades victory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sydie Peck bagged a first-half hat-trick as Sheffield United edged past Preston 3-2 at Deepdale.

The 22-year-old inadvertently equalised with an intended cross in the 27th minute, put his team ahead with a gorgeous second from just outside the box 10 minutes later, and sealed his treble with a tap-in on the stroke of the interval.

Leo Leroy had put the hosts in front after just two minutes with a clinical finish and substitute Callum Lang set up a grandstand finish with a composed 77th-minute consolation.

It is the first time Sheffield United have managed back-to-back wins this season but that makes it just one point out of 18 for new Preston manager Graham Alexander.

North End had made a fantastic start as Andrew Hughes stole the ball off a sleeping Tahith Chong before laying it off to Andrija Vukcevic, whose cutback was scuffed by Andrew Moran but then emphatically slammed home from the centre of the box by Leroy.

Chong nearly atoned for his error inside 10 minutes with a purposeful run and wicked delivery that Ben Brereton Diaz thumped just over the bar on the turn from a similar position to where the goal had been scored.

Preston's strong start was marred by the loss of Johnny Kenny, who left the pitch clutching his hamstring for Lang after just 13 minutes, and the nature of the equaliser was a bitter pill to taste as Peck's teasing cross evaded everyone and sneaked into the far corner.

Charlton 0-1 Bolton: Sam Dalby scores Trotters winner as poor run goes on for Addicks

Birmingham 3-0 Millwall: Alex Cochrane, Max Bird and Jay Stansfield net in Blues win

Derby 0-4 Norwich: More pressure on John Eustace after rampant Canaries win

West Brom 1-1 Southampton: Samuel Edozie earns point for Saints

Blackburn 1-2 Stoke City: Jack McGlynn steers Potters to victory

Portsmouth 3-1 Swansea: Terry Devlin scores twice in Pompey win

There was nothing inadvertent about Peck's 37th-minute second, however, as he nicked the ball away from a stranded Daniel Iversen, chasing Brereton Diaz's ball forward before showing remarkable composure to find the top corner from 20 yards, firing past the despairing Preston keeper and six white and blue shirts that had tried to recover.

In first-half stoppage time, two became three for the homegrown talent and it was a poacher's finish to prod Romelle Donovan's driven cross over the line from point-blank range to put the Blades in control.

Liam Lindsay came on as part of a double change Alexander made at the interval and the 31-year-old was left for dead within minutes as Chong stormed inside from the right before curling just wide, and his rude awakening continued in the 51st minute as Peck nearly placed Hamza Choudhury's tee-up into the net for his fourth, but Iversen parried to safety.

As the game looked like fizzling out for the Lilywhites, two of the substitutes combined when Alfie Devine, who came on for Jusef Erabi just after the hour, rolled the ball across a day-dreaming Blades defence and Lang slotted a first-time effort into the corner, but a comeback never materialised.

"There are times when we might look like we don't care or we're not fully committed but we are. We're just human beings and if you have that period for a long time, six to eight months or something (of struggling) and it can wear you down a bit but it's only us who can get ourselves out of it.

"We have to find a way of creating that mentality, that anger, because that's what I thought we saw in the second half. There was an anger about our team. A controlled anger.

"We conceded a goal and then, I don't think it's an intentional drop of effort, I think it's just a human-nature thing in that we maybe feel a bit sorry for ourselves a little bit and maybe lose a bit of confidence."

"His all-round performance was excellent. (We) were talking about playing him higher, putting him in the box and making forward runs. He's done it right throughout his young career - scored goals - and he needs to score more.

"I spoke to him about Leicester last season, where he got a couple, and he's got that in his locker. He's a touch disappointed because he's had a couple more opportunities in the second half. We got into some great positions.

"(Tahith) Chong should score, Sydie possibly should score, I'm not going to be greedy and say every opportunity we have we should score from but we created enough to take the game away from the opposition. Sydie will get the headlines and rightly so."

#927. Hibs toast win over Hearts - but will they kick on before cup final?

Hibs players joined their fans in a stirring rendition of Sunshine On Leith

Such were Marink Reedijk's wishes, shared in an official Hibernian video, external from the dressing room following their historic Hampden beating of Heart of Midlothian in the Scottish League Cup semi-final.

If the Hibs head coach ventured into Leith on Sunday night he would not have been short of offers for both, as he has instantly scribbled his name into the history books.

His wait for a first win in charge ended at game five. As player of the match Joe Newell said afterwards: "I would have taken four losses if this was the way it clicked."

There was a wee wait for Reedjik to break his Hibs duck, but that is nothing compared to the agony Hibs supporters had endured since 2006 when travelling across the M8 to face their city rivals at the national stadium.

Four visits, four endings with jubilant Jambos. Until now.

The sights and sounds of Sunshine on Leith being belted from the east end of the national stadium will take some time to shift, for this is a win Hibs must savour.

Self-professed "ice king" Reedijk revelled in the iconic anthem but admitted it is his responsibility to make "rational decisions" and so remove himself from the "lovely atmosphere".

He will know he and his players must make this moment the launchpad as they attempt to lift off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership.

After he has enjoyed the tunes and pints, of course.

Hibs edge Hearts in thrilling derby to reach League Cup final

Giant curiosity Hibs finally liberated from the sucker punch

McInnes demands more after delivering Rangers' trophy chance

Who could have thought it would have played out this way?

On the eve of their big trip west, Hibs had slipped - again - to the foot of the league table after Kilmarnock picked up a point at home to the 10 men of St Johnstone.

A shocking place for this squad to be, but it was - temporarily - rendered meaningless 24 hours later.

Given their turbulent start to the season - missing out on Europe, failing to win at home and changing managers - being backed by 19,000 supporters was something in itself.

Finally, they were rewarded. Those who travelled to Warsaw last year to lose out on goal difference to Legia and returned from Gent in August with an abundance of hope only to have it dashed at Easter Road, had their moment of joy. And they rightly milked it.

When Jordi Altena's deep free-kick in the 93rd minute ended in goalkeeper Raphael Sallinger's hands, the roar from the other end of Hampden shook the steps on which Hearts supporters were already hovering in search of a swift exit.

Those clad in maroon - all 23,000 of them present and the many others in Gorgie - are surely the only beings unmoved by the inimitable Sunshine on Leith.

Newell had his hands on his head. Boyhood Hibee Jason Kerr was holding back the tears. Nicky Cadden was singing from chest. Arm in arm, Hibs were a unit, as they were from the minute they conceded.

"I love these kind of things" - Marink Reedijk on spine-tingling rendition of Sunshine on Leith

At that point, Newell - who proceeded to pull the strings - was full of fear.

A simple but strong header from Claudio Braga, before many supporters had even taken to their seats, brought concern.

Could a repeat of that unforgettable afternoon - Hibs supporters aren't allowed to forget it - 14 years ago, when Hearts fired five past them in the Scottish Cup final, be on the cards?

"The game plan was out the window," midfielder Newell said. "It's not ideal, is it?

"You go to bed [on Saturday night] thinking of all the scenarios and the way you dream and imagine the game is going to go and then, after two minutes, they score.

"But I think, if anything, it shows how good the character is and kind of emphasises it was even more of a special performance, not just the win."

Which is, surely, what Reedijk and his team will take out of this the most. Any team can win a cup game, but not any team can show the grit, determination and depth Hibs did in setting up a final against Rangers next month.

The showpiece is six weeks away. Few clubs more than Hibs know how much can change in that time frame.

They have as many league games in that period, with the last - of course - being a dress rehearsal of the final as they welcome Derek McInnes' side to Easter Road.

While those in green and white admitted post-match it would be difficult not to think of their return to Hampden - when they will be aiming for the club's first silverware since beating the Ibrox side in the 2016 Scottish Cup final - they know they need to arrest their current league form.

With just two wins in 11 games, they have a trip to struggling Aberdeen - who lost in Saturday's semi-final - on Saturday before welcoming both Dundee clubs to the capital.

Trips to Motherwell and Kilmarnock respectively follow before that meeting with the Light Blues as they search for some much-needed points.

The hope is this performance and result will kick-start their quest to climb the table.

"It's huge," 33-year-old Newell added. "You kind of forget that there's a cup final after that, do you know what I mean?

"You feel like you want to say, that's it done because it felt massive. These games are always huge no matter where they are, but we have to kick on now.

"We have to use it and hopefully it gives all the boys confidence, because it should do. We were outstanding."

Do that, and repeat this result against Rangers on 13 December, and Reedijk and co will never be left wanting for music and beer in Leith ever again.

#925. QPR battle back to hold Burnley

Queens Park Rangers vs Burnley. Sky Bet Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Queens Park Rangers and Burnley at the MATRADE Loftus Road Stadium on Tuesday night; Jonathan Varane earns point for QPR

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jonathan Varane denied Burnley a first win under new boss Fabio Celestini as QPR fought back for a 1-1 draw.

Largie Ramazani had Burnley dreaming of only their second victory of the season when he fired them ahead at Loftus Road.

But Varane's second-half strike earned Rangers a point, with a little help from Burnley goalkeeper Gregoire Coudert.

The Clarets arrived in west London with one win in 13 Championship games and already on a second manager of the season after Nicky Hayen was sacked last week.

QPR came into the match after a topsy turvy October, hammering Derby 4-1 and Swansea 5-0 at home, while losing 3-0 at Birmingham and, on Saturday, 4-1 at Southampton.

The hosts almost got off to the perfect start after Harvey Vale won a free-kick on the edge of the box, but the midfielder curled his effort inches wide.

Rangers wideman Paul Smyth then cut inside Hjalmar Ekdal only to pull his shot just wide of the near post, before captain Jimmy Dunne's long-range drive cleared the crossbar.

Charlton 0-1 Bolton: Sam Dalby scores Trotters winner as poor run goes on for Addicks

Birmingham 3-0 Millwall: Alex Cochrane, Max Bird and Jay Stansfield net in Blues win

Derby 0-4 Norwich: More pressure on John Eustace after rampant Canaries win

West Brom 1-1 Southampton: Samuel Edozie earns point for Saints

Blackburn 1-2 Stoke City: Jack McGlynn steers Potters to victory

Portsmouth 3-1 Swansea: Terry Devlin scores twice in Pompey win

But out of nothing, Burnley took the lead with seven minutes of a one-sided first half remaining.

Coudert's clearance was met with a poor header from Rangers defender Ronnie Edwards.

Jamie Vardy cleverly worked the second ball out to Leeds loanee Ramazani, who struck a sweet 20-yard drive past Pierce Charles, the Rangers goalkeeper getting a hand to the ball but not keeping it out.

Moments later Vardy thought he had set up a second for Andreas Hountondji, who tucked the ball past Charles only to be flagged offside.

Rangers almost hit back before half-time through Edwards' deflected shot, but Coudert got down to make a fine save.

They should have equalised just after the break when Vale whipped in a free-kick but Dunne uncharacteristically missed a free header.

Rangers boss Julien Stephan made a double change on the hour and the subs almost combined to equalise with their first touches, Rayan Kolli pulling the ball back for Ilias Chair, who blazed over the crossbar.

However, the hosts hauled themselves level in the 65th minute when Chair teed up Varane, whose shot from the edge of the box slipped under Coudert's glove and into the net.

Vardy could have won it for the Clarets - and probably would have done 10 years ago - when he was put through by Hountondji late on.

The 39-year-old former Premier League winner let the ball run across him, but then buried his angled finish into the side-netting.

"I'm frustrated with the result. I enjoyed the performance.

"We should have scored one or two in the first 20 minutes. Then they scored with their first shot and we missed some easy passes.

"In the second half I thought we had the chances not only to equalise but to win. We were really dominant but it's a lack of efficiency which is the difference between us and the teams at the top."

"We were very close to taking three points but when you see the game, one point is good. The team is together and trying to win games.

"We missed a bit of quality. With the ball I think we can do better. But one point, Saturday, one point today, hopefully next we can get three. But at the moment I'm happy with what I see."

#923. Devlin scores twice as Portsmouth beat Swansea

Portsmouth vs Swansea City. Sky Bet Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Portsmouth and Swansea City at Fratton Park on Tuesday night; Terry Devlin scores fine double for Pompey as they claim victory over the Swans.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Terry Devlin's double denied Swansea the chance to take top spot in the Championship as in-form Portsmouth won 3-1 at Fratton Park.

Devlin's first-half goal looked like it was going to be enough for Pompey but Zan Vipotnik, the Championship's top scorer last season, won and converted an 85th-minute penalty to set up a blockbuster finale.

Devlin's smart finish from a corner in the second minute of stoppage time and Tommy Waddingham's strike six minutes later made sure Pompey made it six without defeat, and Middlesbrough - who play on Wednesday - remained at the summit.

The first-half rhythm settled into one where the Swans had nearly all of the ball - ending up with 62 per cent possession - but Pompey had far more shots.

Right-sided winger Adrian Segecic was a constant threat but scuffed an early chance wide after smart interplay with full debutant Odin Bailey. Visiting goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux's first test was an awkward bouncing shot from Tyrese Shade that he pushed behind with his forearm.

Swansea lost Stephen Welsh to a leg injury but finally managed to put together an attack and shot in the 26th minute - but Nicolas Schmid was hardly tested by Jay Fulton's effort.

The deadlock was broken in the 36th minute by Devlin, but it owed a lot to Segecic's industry down the right.

Charlton 0-1 Bolton: Sam Dalby scores Trotters winner as poor run goes on for Addicks

Birmingham 3-0 Millwall: Alex Cochrane, Max Bird and Jay Stansfield net in Blues win

The Croatian burst down the wing and after his first attempt at a cross was blocked, his second found Bailey. The ball bounced off him and into Devlin's path to nudge home his third of the season.

Swansea's response almost saw an equaliser when a free-kick on the edge of the box was slid to Goncalo Franco and his fizzed shot deflected narrowly over the bar.

The hosts were aggrieved they had a second goal ruled out just after the hour mark. Marko Milovanovic tapped home but a foul was given against Segecic on Jenson Seelt - although replays showed a slip rather than a tackle.

The visitors became more and more dangerous as the second half progressed but had to wait until the 85th minute to score. Vipotnik went down in the box after Regan Poole had grabbed his shirt, before the Slovenian stepped up to convert.

Swansea should have overtaken Boro and grabbed a winner in the 88th minute but Ross Stewart squandered a simple chance and instead hit the crossbar.

They were made to rue the big miss when Devlin gathered Bailey's corner, spun and found the bottom corner.

Waddingham added further gloss even deeper into stoppage time when he bullied Ben Cabango and slotted away as Portsmouth made it four wins in six to go 10th.

"It is a massive win and an important night for us for a number of reasons.

"I am delighted with the result, it is a brilliant result and we would have taken that all day.

"I thought we were absolutely superb in what we wanted to execute for 48 minutes of the game. I was disappointed with the way we conceded the penalty but to respond as we did was magnificent.

"With the way the game had gone we were on the back foot but we looked dangerous on the counter and always thought there was still something there. We were trying to be as attacking as possible and always felt there was another goal there."

"It wasn't easy at the end but we want to be a team that stays emotionally balanced and calm in every situation. That is something we can improve. We are all humans and there wasn't a player that didn't want to win.

"In a hard game we got it back to 1-1 and felt we could still win the game still. That is the mindset we need to have. We need to stay stable and remain focused on all the details of the game.

"It is not an easy place to come and hold the emotions. It's a hard league and there are so many games to come. It is important we keep focus on what we need to improve and do better."

#922. Former Rangers player Kyle Hutton to stand trial over road death

Victoria Cairns died four days after the crash in Rutherglen in November 2024

Former Rangers player Kyle Hutton is to stand trial in 2028 accused of killing a woman in a road collision.

Hutton is said to have been "unfit to drive through alcohol or drugs" when he allegedly struck Victoria Cairns, 40, in Farmeloan Road, Rutherglen, South Lanarkshire, on 2 November 2024.

The 35-year-old denies the charges, which include going at excessive speed for the conditions at the time and not seeing the pedestrian.

Cairns died from her injuries in hospital four days later.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Hutton faces a charge of causing death by dangerous driving, and other charges of failing to co-operate with breath and drug tests and not providing two specimens of breath to determine his "ability to drive".

There is an alternative allegation that the fatality was as a result of Hutton - who played for the Ibrox club between 2010 and 2015 - being careless behind the wheel.

Prosecutors state Hutton failed to carry out "proper observations" and did not detect Cairns standing on the road.

It is alleged he then struck the woman, causing her to fall to the ground and that she was so badly hurt she died in hospital four days later.

During a hearing at the High Court in Glasgow Graeme Brown KC, defending, pleaded not guilty on Hutton's behalf.

The solicitor advocate added there was potentially upsetting footage which jurors may be shown as part of the evidence.

He also said Hutton's wife was likely to be called as a defence witness.

Lord Scott went on to set a trial, which could last about four days, for 7 February 2028.

Hutton, whose other clubs included St Mirren, Dumbarton and Partick Thistle, remains on bail meantime.

#920. Wagner brothers begin new NBA chapter on different paths

After five years, brothers Franz and Moritz Wagner are no longer playing together for the Orlando Magic. In the new NBA season, their separation will likely mean the new "German" team is the Charlotte Hornets.

In 2021, when Franz Wagner joined the Orlando Magic to start his NBA career, his older brother Moritz was already on the team. Franz, who is four years younger, was selected eighth overall in the draft by the team who had signed Moritz a few months earlier.

It's not just their joint appearances in the NBA that have since turned the "Wagners" into something of a brand in basketball. Just last year, the NBA had a regular-season game in Berlin, partly because of the Wagner brothers.

Moritz is a successful podcast host and often has his brother on the show. Both have their own Instagram accounts, each with around 300,000 followers. In 2024, the German public broadcaster ZDF aired a four-part TV documentary about the brothers, chronicling their basketball history and close relationship.

In recent years, they've also celebrated success with the German national team. In 2023, they became world champions together and were then at the Olympic Games in Paris a year later. In 2025, Franz also won the European Championship title, while Moritz, sidelined by injury, watched on as a TV analyst.

This summer, their time together came to an end. After Moritz wasn't offered a new contract in Orlando, he accepted an offer from the Brooklyn Nets. He now lives in New York with his girlfriend, Maggie McQuade, who works in marketing for the NBA.

"I've already spent a lot of time in New York. It's kind of like my home in America," Wagner said on his podcast, adding that it reminds him of where he's from. "As far as the US goes, Brooklyn is actually very close to Berlin."

The call from the Nets proved a stroke of luck. "When we hung up the phone and both agreed, we both cried. Because you kind of realize that this move feels right somehow," Wagner said. "We're just staying home."

The Nets are considered one of the weaker teams heading into the upcoming season, leaving Wagner a key force in providing stability and helping to develop younger players.

Franz is staying in Orlando. Alongside Paolo Banchero, Franz is one of the team's two stars. The 25-year-old is on a massive contract that runs through 2030 and will earn him a reported total of $224 million (€199 million).

With Sean Sweeney hired as their new head coach for the upcoming season, the Magic are hoping to finally advance past the first round of the playoffs, having lost at that stage in each of the last three seasons.

Success is expected to come from a faster style of basketball than has been played in Orlando in recent years. In the new system, Franz Wagner will take on the role of point guard more prominently than before — moving the ball up the court, creating his own shots, and driving to the basket with speed — much like he does for Germany.

"We want to play tough, play together, play it fast and enjoy playing together," Wagner said during a preseason interview. "We got a little bit more space for our guys, to get in the paint and make plays, for themselves and for others."

However, he now has to manage without his older brother.

"I think we're both a little sad his time here has come to an end," Franz Wagner said in an interview with sports news site ClutchPoints. "I think, though, we're both really grateful for the time we had [together]. To play with a sibling in the NBA for so many years is super special. So we're just grateful for that."

Now that the Wagners’ time together in Orlando is history, German basketball fans may have to adjust their allegiances a bit for the upcoming season.

While many Germans became fans of the Dallas Mavericks during the era of German basketball icon Dirk Nowitzki, and interest in the Orlando Magic has been particularly high in recent years, that interest may spread in the coming season. A total of eight Germans are under contract on an NBA team for the 2026/27 season:

While Hartenstein, who won the NBA championship with the Thunder in 2025, has another shot at the title, Hukporti, now in Philadelphia, tore his Achilles tendon in the first preseason game and will be out for the entire season. The Sixers have signed NBA legend LeBron James and are considered one of the title contenders.

Maxi Kleber, a reliable bench player for the past nine years, did not receive a new contract from the Los Angeles Lakers and is currently a free agent.

The Charlotte Hornets could then become Germany's new favorite NBA team, with Germany captain and NBA nomad Dennis Schröder now on the roster. In his 14th year in the NBA, the Hornets are already his 12th different team.

Playing alongside him will be two German rookies, highly-touted Hannes Steinbach and Christian Anderson Jr. The two newcomers know each other from the German U19 national team, with which they won the silver medal at the 2025 World Championship.

"I'm a veteran — I've been in the league for 14 years now, I've actually been with the team the longest — and of course I'm trying to guide these two young guys through their rookie season and make it as easy as possible for them,” Schröder recently said in an interview with RTL/Sky Sport.

"It's really cool to have someone like that here. Dennis, of course, has already played a lot of games in the NBA," Steinbach said. "You have someone there you can speak German with, who gives you a few tips based on what he sees during the game."

The Hornets are aiming to make the playoffs at the end of the season. Since they play in the Eastern Conference, just like Brooklyn and Orlando, there will be plenty of matchups against the other German players along the way.

This article was originally written in German.

#919. Bolton earn narrow win at struggling Charlton

Charlton Athletic vs Bolton Wanderers. Sky Bet Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Charlton Athletic and Bolton Wanderers at The Valley on Tuesday night; Sam Dalby scores the Trotters winner as Addicks misery continues.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sam Dalby's sixth goal of the season earned Bolton a 1-0 victory at misfiring Charlton.

The result piles more pressure on Addicks boss Nathan Jones with the south-east Londoners now winless in 11 matches, and a fourth straight Championship loss dropped them to 21st in the table.

Bolton captain Josh Sheehan pulled the midfield strings during the opening 45 minutes and produced a whipped shot wide after five minutes.

Charlton had the first of the minimal openings in the first half on seven minutes. Tyreece Campbell's deep cross picked out Danny McNamara's run to the far post but the right-sided wing-back's attempt to convert was frustrated by Wanderers goalkeeper Jack Bonham.

Charlie Kelman had the ball in the net for the hosts soon after but it was flagged offside.

Bolton went ahead in the 18th minute. Nathaniel Chalobah's misplaced pass gifted Dalby a run on goal and the striker confidently finished past Will Mannion.

Charlton were unable to force Bonham into a save during the first period, aside from a comfortable claim from a tame Kelman attempt early on. Harvey Knibbs headed harmlessly wide from Karlan Grant's cross.

Birmingham 3-0 Millwall: Alex Cochrane, Max Bird and Jay Stansfield net in Blues win

Derby 0-4 Norwich: More pressure on John Eustace after rampant Canaries win

West Brom 1-1 Southampton: Samuel Edozie earns point for Saints

Blackburn 1-2 Stoke City: Jack McGlynn steers Potters to victory

Portsmouth 3-1 Swansea: Terry Devlin scores twice in Pompey win

Preston 2-3 Sheffield United: Sydie Peck's hat-trick sees Blades to victory

It needed Charlton skipper Lloyd Jones to make a vital block on Max Conway's shot after McNamara lost possession inside the penalty box.

The home support booed their team off at half-time, voicing their frustrations as the Addicks, clearly lacking in confidence, moved the ball too slowly.

Bolton midfielder Atsuki Ito smashed a first time volley wide of the right upright early in the second half.

Kelman produced a first-time header from a decent left wing delivery by Campbell on the hour mark. It proved to be the forward's last action as he was replaced by veteran Matty Godden.

Bonham was penalised for picking up Sheehan's backpass but Wanderers were out quickly to block Knibbs' shot from eight yards out from Grant's short free-kick.

Charlton exerted pressure as the contest wore on but Bolton defended resiliently, typified by a strong display from Akin Famewo, who was also close at the other end of the pitch to connecting with Gaizka Larrazabal's free-kick.

Wanderers substitute Thierry Gale twice had opportunities to finish the contest off but could not beat Mannion.

Campbell sent a 20-yard curler wide at the other end as Bolton picked up a third win in a four-match unbeaten sequence on the road.

"In terms of endeavour, work-rate and passing the football I have zero problem. We have had so many opportunities around the edge of the box.

"We had no problem all night and then we gifted them a goal. They haven't had to work for it in any way. We then did not demonstrate enough attacking quality in the final third.

"We've probably made more positive substitutions tonight than is humanly possible - I got as many attacking players on the pitch. We aren't doing the out-of-possession stuff well enough either and that is a tough recipe.

"All we can do is more work, big them up, give them a cuddle - we do it. We ask them to hit areas and be confident. We work on the final third and know how we can get in behind them and we just don't do it when we cross the white line.

"We have won games here with a lot less possession and a lot less opportunities in the final third."

"It's a huge result for us. It is never easy to get three points away from home on a Tuesday night fixture, especially after a setback for us on Saturday.

"We deserved to win that game and let it slip. It was important we tried to respond and we did that tonight.

"We knew it would be a difficult game with everything going on here. They are not in a great run of form, so we expected them to throw everything at us and we dealt with that really well, especially in the first half when we were nice and calm.

"We've had about seven one-v-ones this season and that's the first one we've been able to take. So there was a bit of doubt - until he hit the net. He took it well. It was a mistake and we managed to pounce on it.

"It gave the players some belief and confidence that we could go and get a result here."

#918. The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson

There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment

And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically?

It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.

In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.

Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full story is explored by the journalist David Walsh here).

It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.

Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.

Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.

The problem was that Glazer and his family would prove some of the worst club owners in English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

A mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.

#917. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#916. Rodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes on | Moving the Goalposts

Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes sense

When Washington plays Chicago this Sunday in DC, “Rowdy Audi” will probably be full. It will also be full when the post-season starts, should they lock up their top-four position with a positive result on Decision Day. Equipped with an accessible stadium in a big city, a proud fanbase and a formidable roster rife with players qualifying for the High Impact Player (HIP) rule’s initial criteria (including Trinity Rodman, who gave the rule its moniker), the Spirit hold sway in the attendance charts.

But starting next season, everyone on the Spirit will qualify for the “Rodman Rule”. So will every player in NWSL. Announced Friday, NWSL settled a grievance with the league’s Players Association, who argued that the initial criteria violated federal labor law.

Admittedly, when the new policy arrived on the scene last winter, it appeared half-baked, a somewhat frantic attempt to keep Rodman from floating across the Atlantic and doing something terrible, like playing for Michele Kang’s London City Lionesses instead of Michele Kang’s Washington Spirit.

A rule was born to prevent that. It allocated added funds beyond the salary cap for players who met league-set criteria that clearly prioritized international name recognition in a global market. Qualifying players needed to meet one of eight categories including SportsPro Media’s top 150 Most Marketable Athletes (only Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmatí placed in 2026, though 16 female football players did in 2025, including three in the NWSL at the time – Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson and Marta, in that order). It also included ESPN’s Top 50, the Guardian’s top 100, top minutes on the US national team, the Ballon d’Or’s 30-player list, or NWSL’s MVP and Best XI awards.

Some measure of umbrage followed, as invested onlookers argued for a simpler solution: just raise the salary cap. And perhaps they should, but keeping an American-style sports league competitive in a global football landscape is less straightforward. The looming spectre of Europe’s super-teams, who have attracted key members of the USWNT starting XI, is ever present, waiting to take Croix Bethune away for the right amount of money. No doubt, the NWSL’s appeal is evident in its expansion and growth, in the success of its spine of stateside stalwarts, in its rapidly expanding dedicated facilities, and in the international talents such as Esme Morgan or Ann-Katrin Berger that choose to sharpen their skills in the US.

However, the domestic sporting culture of the NWSL is somewhat at odds, in some ways a disadvantage, when it comes to maintaining its margins, with a stand-alone team structure in a parity-driven league, while competing for international glory with teams such as Chelsea, Lyon or Barcelona, who spend three times or more the amount that some NWSL teams do. While competing for status as the world’s go-to destination, for players and fans, glory hunting and name recognition do matter.

Just look at the Ballon d’Or: Barcelona’s women took all but one of the awards available to them, though Alexia Putellas, who collected her third main prize, now plays in London. That Putellas deserves her trophy is not in dispute, though the inequitable factors contributing to international accolades were manifest. Putellas starred for two super-teams: Barcelona and Spain. Ewa Pajor, Barcelona’s Polish striker, fell just short, perhaps edged out by only having one super-team to play for.

Subtly, it seemed, the original criteria for the HIP rule flirted with the idea of fostering a super-team in the US. Prior to the update, there was no cap on the number of players who could access the extra million if the salary cap was already met. For a team such as Kang’s in Washington, the door felt open, possibly, to building a team even more ready to contend with the heavy spenders in Europe (including those also funded by Kang), and the international accolades that go with it. If a NWSL player lifted the NWSL trophy, helped win January’s inaugural Club World Cup, then performed well at the World Cup, could a second NWSL (active) player win the Ballon d’Or?

The structure of the HIP rule remains in place. Teams that have met 2027’s salary cap of $4.4m (£3.3m) in 2027 can spend an additional $1.257m (as reported by ESPN) on a player. The post-grievance difference is that teams can spend that additional sum on any player. Gone are the stipulations mandating adherence to that eight-criteria list of global recognition.

The change is a win for players that did not meet it, which includes elite players who fell short in previous seasons (such as Ashley Sanchez) or star players with long-lasting or recurring injuries (Catarina Macario). It gives the NWSL’s individual teams the autonomy to decide which players are worthy, based on whatever criteria they see fit. And, with a cap on the number of players that can access it, it gives cash-strapped teams the theoretical ability to rein in teams with already-stacked rosters.

But the spirit of NWSL’s original criteria has more merit than many suggest. The NWSL is responsible for securing overhead issues such as an improved media rights deal, marketing marquee names to broadcasters, ensuring the league is seen as the go-to destination before a World Cup and performing well in global cup competitions such as the Concacaf W Champions Cup (Mexico’s Club América prevailed in the most recent final) or the upcoming Club World Cup. With that in mind – plus the ever-pressing desire to keep USWNT players in the US – the original HIP criteria had its eye on awarding stardom as it’s seen in the global market.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Stardom is imprecise. It’s hard to measure, but impossible to miss. Rodman did not make the Ballon d’Or shortlist and is not leading the Golden Boot race. But Rodman and her closest national team peers (including “Triple Espresso” compadres Mallory Swanson and Wilson) are the presumed stars of the NWSL. Rodman, alongside Wilson (who clocked the Michael Jordan “shrug” celebration after scoring in the 2022 Championship final) have not just the skill but the personality flourishes reminiscent of Alex Morgan sipping the tea in Lyon.

The NWSL has yet to replicate the Morgan effect (think default attendance records and adoring away fans), but requiring that teams reward players with a certain je ne sais quoi in their international football fame was baked into the league’s original attempt at the HIP criteria.

#913. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#912. Football Daily | Aston Villa, ‘unacceptable insults’ and thin-skinned clutching of pearls

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

When Jamie Carragher appeared as a pundit on Sky Sports Super Sunday, Football Daily was surprised he didn’t have a solicitor sitting alongside him, occasionally jotting notes on a pad or leaning over to give whispered instructions and answer “no comment” to any leading questions about Trey Nyoni starting ahead of Ryan Gravenberch. On Friday night, the former Liverpool defender was subjected to a threat of legal action from Aston Villa, who took such grave exception to some “unacceptable insults” he had rained down on them from his podcast pulpit, that they were ready to call in the heavy legal artillery and stop him from preventing their “ascension in English and European football”. Taking a leaf out of the tried-and-much-ridiculed Nottingham Forest playbook, Villa chair Nassef Sawiris appears to have eschewed contacting Carragher through the usual formal channels and instead cajoled some unfortunate junior comms staffer to make the portentous announcement on their Social Media Disgraces.

Villa’s threat came on the back of some fairly obvious observations he made on Stick To Football, when he pointed out that English football has a food-chain and despite their commendable successes in recent seasons, Villa aren’t quite as high up it as the richest man in Egypt might like to think. During a debate about the likelihood of Unai Emery leaving Villa to take over the soon-to-be-vacant head coach’s job at Manchester United, Carragher had said the Spaniard would “want that opportunity to manage a giant again”, before pointing out “there is a chain in football, whether you like it or not”. As controversial footballing takes go, it was right up there with pointing out that bears defecate in the woods and Pope Leo XIV wears a funny hat. “So shut the [eff] up Aston Villa fans,” honked Carragher, hitting his stride. “Aston Villa will never be Manchester United.”

Of course, with this being football, there is always a danger that explicitly signposted and totally anodyne badinage will inevitably be misinterpreted by thin-skinned folk who are desperate to be offended. But it is usually self-professed terminally-online superfans, not multi-billionaire club chairs whose hands instinctively reach for their pearls. While it remains unclear what exactly it was he said that was actionable, Carragher subsequently apologised for his comments. “I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans,” he trumpeted from his soapbox in the digital town square. “My language this week was clumsy & wrong. I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV!”

It has now been reported that Villa have dropped their threat of unspecified legal action against Carragher but it remains to be seen if Fulham can look forward to hearing from their lawyers after helping to prevent their ascension up the league after [Snip! Snip! Snippety-snip! – Football Daily Lawyers] at Villa Park on Saturday night.

Join Daniel Harris from 8pm GMT for hot minute-by-minute updates from Newcastle 2-1 Everton in the Premier League, for which Jack Grealish will again be absent.

Sport in Focus picks out the best images from the past week and delivers them, along with the stories behind them, to your inbox every Friday. It’s great and well worth your time subscribing to. Right. Here.

“I’m not always showing my emotions, but it’s really touching. So maybe it looks like I’m an ‘ice king’, so to say. Normally in Holland we say ‘ice queen’, but therefore an ice king because I’m not a woman. But for me, it is really important that this happens and it comes close to my heart. Guys who inspire people on the pitch with something people off the pitch and in the stands love to see. That is what football is about” – Hibs head coach Marink Reedijk gets emotional after watching fans’ rendition of Sunshine on Leith, in the wake of their 2-1 Skol Cup semi-final win over Hearts at Hampden.

double quotation markOK. I know readers are going to say I’m only writing about this because I’m a Liverpool fan and VAR looked the other way when a clear and obvious shirt pull prevented Alexander Isak from a free header a few yards from goal. But, every week, a different team has a similar beef while commentators debate over whether the shirt was held for long enough, as if there were a time limit stated in the rulebook. And the infuriating thing is that unlike pushing and tripping fouls, no refereeing judgment should be required: it’s either a fist-full of shirt or it’s not. And unlike handballs, shirt pulls are always intentional and always illegal. So, if I had a spare £1.057bn or so and could buy a team, I’d outfit my players in paper-thin jerseys that would tear away without holding them back. Better league-wide solutions would not be hard to imagine or implement, but no, the Premier League must clearly feel that refereeing controversies are one of the sport’s main attractions and probably can point to social media disgraces as evidence. The beautiful game?” – Steve Plever.

double quotation markFriday’s Football Daily letters gave us offerings from L Json and Stewart McGuiness, which caused me to wonder who would be the recipient of the coveted prizeless prize. Scrolling slowly down, I was shocked. Nothing. Not even a benign ‘rollover’ announcement. Just … nothing. Beyond ruining the weekend for the 1,057 regulars, imagine the pain this inflicted on your contributors all weekend long” – Peter Rehwaldt (and 1,056 others) [our apologies; by way of contrition, we now have prizes all this week – Football Daily Ed].
