#844. Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family

Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture

Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

#843. This cholesterol drug promised to be a game-changer. Why did it flop in the clinic — and is there still hope?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cassandra Willyard is a science journalist in Madison, Wisconsin.

Lipoprotein(a) is a cholesterol-carrying molecule that raises the risk of cardiovascular disease. Credit: Juan Gaertner/Science Photo Library

In early September, pharmaceutical giant Novartis issued a press release that sent shock waves through the cardiology community. A drug called pelacarsen, once expected to be a potential blockbuster, had failed to reduce the risk of heart problems and stroke in people with underlying cardiovascular disease.

More muscle, less belly fat: mutations to a gene are linked to wide-ranging benefits

More muscle, less belly fat: mutations to a gene are linked to wide-ranging benefits

Michelle O’Donoghue, a cardiologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts, says her initial reaction to the news was “a state of disbelief”.

Pelacarsen lowers the levels of a type of cholesterol-carrying molecule called lipoprotein(a), often referred to as Lp(a) or Lp little a. Similar to low-density lipoprotein, or LDL, high levels of Lp(a) increase the risk of heart attacks and other heart-related problems. But unlike LDL (sometimes called bad cholesterol), Lp(a) levels are determined mostly by genetics, rather than lifestyle. So, the roughly one in five people who have high Lp(a) levels cannot reduce them through changes in diet and exercise. And although people can lower their LDL levels with statins and other medications, there are no approved drugs that substantially lower Lp(a).

That is why cardiologists were so excited about pelacarsen and a handful of other Lp(a)-lowering drugs that are currently in late-stage clinical trials. “Lp(a) has really been the talk of the town over the past several years in the cardiovascular community, in part because of a lot of enthusiasm over these therapies,” says O’Donoghue, who is an investigator on one of the trials. The therapies lower Lp(a) by 80% or more. All researchers had to prove was that this reduction leads to better clinical outcomes — fewer heart-related deaths, heart attacks, strokes and emergency bypass surgeries.

Why the trial, known as Lp(a)HORIZON, failed isn’t yet clear (see go.nature.com/4sv4ekx). Novartis representatives did not reply to a request for comments. But the high-profile miss has cardiologists questioning what they know about the relationship between Lp(a) and major heart-related problems, and wondering whether other Lp(a)-lowering therapies will meet a similar fate. The US drug firms Amgen and Eli Lilly have large trials under way to test therapies that target Lp(a) using a different approach.

“We had hoped that this would be the first step into a big new area of therapy,” says Harpreet Bhatia, a cardiologist at the University of California, San Diego. Now, he and other researchers are awaiting further details on the Novartis trial and the results from other trials to see whether there is still a future for such approaches to reducing Lp(a).

Lp(a) and LDL both carry cholesterol, a fatty substance that is produced mostly in the liver. The body needs cholesterol, but when its levels are high, it can be deposited in artery walls and form hard plaques, a process known as atherosclerosis. These plaques can grow so thick that they choke off blood flow or rupture, causing blood clots that can prompt a heart attack.

Study after study has shown that people with higher Lp(a) levels are at greater risk of coronary events such as heart attacks, heart-valve problems and heart failure than are individuals with lower levels1. And over the past 30 years, genetic data have bolstered the idea that Lp(a) is not just a marker of risk, but also a causal factor2. “Genetically, I don’t think you could ask for better evidence for this as a drug target,” says Børge Nordestgaard, a cardiologist at the University of Copenhagen and president of the European Atherosclerosis Society in Gothenburg, Sweden.

Structurally, Lp(a) isn’t much different from LDL. Both are essentially globs of fat surrounded by a protein called apolipoprotein B (see ‘Stopping lipoprotein(a)’). Both are produced in the liver. There is, however, one major difference. Lp(a) has a tail composed of apolipoprotein(a), which loops in segments called ‘kringles’ — named after the twists of a Scandinavian pastry. Lp(a) levels depend, in part, on the number of copies of a particular type of kringle encoded in the gene for apolipoprotein(a). People carry anywhere from 1 to more than 40 copies; the fewer the copies, the smaller the particle, and the higher the Lp(a) level. That is because liver cells seem to have an easier time producing and secreting the smaller particles.

Researchers are still trying to unpack how that structural difference affects the particle’s function and its role in cardiovascular disease. Particle for particle, Lp(a) carries six times the risk that LDL does. That could be because it’s more effective at depositing cholesterol on artery walls, or because it promotes inflammation, which can contribute to plaque deposition. But Nordestgaard thinks it has more to do with the impact of Lp(a) on blood clotting. The particle’s tail might make it more difficult for the body to break down clots, which could lead to larger blockages.

Many countries recommend that adults get their Lp(a) levels tested at least once. European atherosclerosis and cardiology societies first recommended that physicians test Lp(a) levels in 2019, and earlier this year, those in the United States followed suit. Because there is no approved therapy for lowering Lp(a), the standard of care for people with high levels is to aggressively reduce other risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

But high Lp(a) levels don’t always cause problems. Bhatia says that sometimes older people have high Lp(a) levels but never have a cardiovascular event. “And sometimes we don’t even see plaque when we look with imaging,” he says. “It may just be that it’s the overall picture of risk, and that Lp(a) is just one piece of that bigger puzzle.”

#841. Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return

Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural Under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.

That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But this is poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.

"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."

FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers." It also said that the winner of the top tier will be crowned champions but all teams will play matches until the tournament concludes on October 30.

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

#840. Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos, FA and coach Tony Popovic at crossroads | Joey Lynch

The most immediate question thrown up by the delay of the tournament in Saudi Arabia is what it now means for Popovic

Confirmation that the Asian Cup has been postponed until December 2027 would have caught few by surprise. But the timing of Tuesday’s announcement might have, given it came well ahead of the late November timeframe hinted at by the AFC. Yet with Houthi attacks continuing across Saudi Arabia, it felt inevitable the tournament would be deferred.

However foreseeable though, it has left the Socceroos, their coach Tony Popovic and Football Australia at a crossroads.

It is a major tournament the Socceroos harboured hopes of winning. Japan would have been considered favourites; the Samurai Blue, despite having been underachievers since winning in 2011, have earned that mantle. But, despite back-to-back quarter-final exits, Australia are also acknowledged as a continental heavyweight by their peers, coming off a World Cup in which they were one of only two Asian sides to progress to the knockout stages. And with rivals such as Qatar, South Korea and Iran all aging and/or experiencing significant upheaval, the regional picture suggested they should have challenged in January.

Popovic would have been able to take to Saudi Arabia a side brimming with young talent and boasting an enviable combination of consistent improvement and valuable World Cup experience. They would have been building on an October window in which they twice met Brazil and a pair of ideal preparatory games against the 2023 Asian Cup finalists, Qatar and Jordan, in November.

Even with fitness concerns hovering over Mohamed Touré and Jordy Bos, the talent and momentum was there for the Socceroos to win a second Asian crown.

Nonetheless, there are silver linings. The tournament may benefit from a 12-month delay, as it will feel less like a post-World Cup afterthought. The postponement could also allow the Socceroos to further evolve and become even better by Christmas next year.

Another 11 months means further development, both for the Socceroos as a collective and for individuals such as Nestory Irankunda, Paul Okon-Engstler, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington. Following their recent high-profile moves to some of Europe’s biggest clubs and leagues, that progression could be significant. It also allows for injured players such as Bos, Touré and Lewis Miller time to recover, while other youngsters yet to establish themselves get more time to impress.

In this scenario, the hope is that a bird in the hand isn’t worth two in the bush – that more injuries don’t strike and that veterans such as Jackson Irvine and Aziz Behich maintain their current form.

But the more immediate question arising from the announcement is what it means for Popovic. The November window is now ostensibly the 53-year-old’s last as Socceroos coach; the contract extension he signed ahead of the World Cup, which was supposed to take him through this tournament, concludes on a definitive date rather than a nebulous “post Asian Cup” marker.

Popovic and Football Australia face a challenge neither would have expected when they hammered out – at the coach’s insistence – a deal that only took him through to the end of the continental showpiece. A similar scenario confronts Graham Arnold with Iraq, while Japan have already signalled that Hajime Moriyasu will be replaced by Go Oiwa.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

Is it now simply a matter of extending Popovic’s deal through to 21 January 2028? Given the federation offered him that longer-term deal, and executives such as Heather Garriock and Martin Kugeler have never been anything but effusive in their praise, it’s almost certain Popovic would be able to if he wants. But does he?

He would have had his reasons for not wanting to be locked into a longer-term deal. And as a football-obsessed workhorse, it’s entirely possible he’d have ambitions to return to the grind of club football. His stock is high after leading the Socceroos to the World Cup’s knockout stages, and further bolstered by a window where his side performed well against Brazil and he drew praise from Carlo Ancelotti. If he wants a new challenge, he has earned one.

But what if he stays, only to depart after another 12 months? Kevin Muscat has always appeared to be an obvious successor, especially given he’ll be a free agent after the imminent conclusion of the Chinese Super League. And if Popovic does opt to depart, he should be offered the job. But would he – or another preferred candidate – be willing to wait a year, especially with World Cup qualification will still beginning in September? Does Football Australia risk being left to scramble come 2028 if they don’t play their cards right?

Just like seemingly everything else in Australian football, the postponement of the Asian Cup presents as both a potential opportunity and a curse.

#839. Dazn secures exclusive deal on global streaming rights for 2029 Club World Cup

Deal deepens company’s relationship with Fifa

Dazn paid $1bn for global rights for the 2025 tournament

Dazn has secured an exclusive option for global streaming rights for the next men’s Club World Cup in 2029 in a development that deepens its partnership with Fifa.

The Saudi Arabia-backed ­streaming company came to Fifa’s aid before the inaugural 32-team Club World Cup in the US last year by agreeing to pay $1bn (£745m) for global rights for the tournament after many ­linear broadcasters and other streamers had declined to bid.

Apple TV had held talks with Fifa over a global streaming deal for 2025, but withdrew owing to a disagreement over valuation, and Fifa’s subsequent attempt to sell the rights on a regional basis foundered.

Dazn’s surprise late bid, facilitated by the purchase of a 10% stake in the company by Saudi’s Surj Sports Investment group, in effect bankrolled Fifa’s $1bn prize fund, with the winners, Chelsea, taking home about $114m (£85m).

Dazn is a loss-making business despite having more than 300 ­million registered users, with its 2025 accounts showing its operating losses increased from $772.9m to $939.8m over the previous 12 months, but appears content to continue to invest heavily in rights.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The value of its Club World Cup rights deal, or the point at which the option must be triggered, is not known but will give Fifa breathing space before the second edition of its expanded competition that has been designed as a major money ­spinner but remains fraught with political problems.

Planning for the 2029 tournament has proved difficult, with no decisions made on venues, format or size despite longstanding discussions between Fifa and the clubs about expanding to 48 teams, first reported by the Guardian two years ago.

Club World Cup progress has been a casualty of the fallout from Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off proposal, which led the lobby group European Football Clubs to threaten to withdraw its support. In a letter to Fifa obtained by the Guardian, EFC also expressed “serious concern and disappointment” at the delays in paying $250m in solidarity money owed to clubs from 2025 more than a year after the first competition had concluded.

Relations between EFC and Fifa are understood to have improved since the withdrawal of Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise plan, but they have yet to agree the finer details of a proposed joint venture to manage the Club World Cup’s commercial operations, which may be put on hold until after the Fifa presidential election in March.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The 2030 men’s World Cup co-host Morocco will be ­favourite to host in 2029 if Infantino is re-elected given his close relationship with King Mohammed VI.

Fifa’s decision to award hosting rights to the first women’s Club World Cup to the US, revealed by the Guardian last month, has strengthened Morocco’s case because the US was in the running for 2029.

A jointly-hosted tournament staged by Morocco and Spain is another possibility. Portugal, the third major 2030 co-host, is understood to have reservations about holding the event.

#837. Cunha completes wild Man Utd comeback win over Roma from two down

Manchester United vs Roma. UEFA Champions League.

Match report as Manchester United beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League despite being two goals down at half-time. Bruno Fernandes scored a penalty and Matheus Cunha scored two to complete the comeback before being sent off late on

Football Features Writer @ghostgoal

Manchester United produced an extraordinary comeback from two down to beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford and pick up their first win in 10 games.

Michael Carrick looked on the brink when his disjointed team were completely undone for Matias Soule's opener and Donyell Malen soon made it two from the penalty spot. But Matheus Cunha won one of his own, scored two and was sent off in a wild contest.

United had been booed off at the break and when Carlos Baleba had to go off early in the second half with a hamstring injury it all looked dismal for United. But when Cunha won a penalty that Bruno Fernandes scored after a retake it altered the momentum.

Bryan Mbeumo struck both posts with one shot soon after and the noise inside Old Trafford was astonishing thereafter. Roma cleared one off the line and United had two more penalty shouts as the Italian side - unbeaten in Serie A - began to wobble badly.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leonardo Balerdi's error proved it, his woeful clearance allowing Cunha to slot home the leveller. And it was the same player with a stunning near-post finish from Shea Lacey's pass who completed the comeback to the delight of the disbelieving crowd.

Cunha was sent off for a silly foul to ensure a tense finale but United held on for a first win in 54 days. Improbably, Carrick left the pitch not just to applause but having presided over a win in the Champions League. And a spirited one at that.

Where on earth did that come from? Roma were two up and it could have been more against a United side whose spirit appeared as broken as their tactics in a first half that seemed like surrender. But strange things can still happen at the Theatre of Dreams.

It is difficult to overstate the incoherence of those opening minutes. Watching Fernandes throw his arms in the air in disgust at a Baleba pass late in the first half, it looked like a team in disarray and desperate to blame someone else for the situation.

United's tactical setup early on against Roma was arguably even worse than against Como when Fernandes criticised his manager. They were continually cut apart in the left-back position with Diogo Dalot up the pitch and Ayden Heaven exposed.

At that stage, thought turned to the balance of the squad and the quality of it, the confidence and the team spirit, the players, the coach and the ownership. None of that completely goes away after a chaotic 45 minutes but this was at least something.

It was a team telling the fans that they can show spirit, that they are not prepared to let it slide further without a fight, that they can still conjure quality from nowhere. The scenes at the end of the game showed that at this great club, sometimes, that can be enough.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes speaking to Amazon Prime:

"Fans want to win games, they've been used to seeing this club at the top, winning trophies, winning games every week. For them it's been so frustrating to see the club in this situation.

"I just want to make everyone aware that we're all frustrated with the situation at the moment and we all want to get out of this. Hopefully this win today gives the start of something good for us.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It has been tough, there's been a lot of speculation in the media, a lot of lies around many things that have happened in this club. Between me and the manager, that we had cleared the air, then after, nothing of that happened.

"The manager took a decision of putting myself on the bench [against Bournemouth] because I wasn't performing at that level. Everyone felt that that was a punishment for the words that I had. If it was, it was right.

"The manager is the one that makes the decisions. I have to accept them, I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, in the staff and every player that is in this club.

"It doesn't change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me. It should be [a turning point]."

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick speaking in the press conference:

"Proud of a lot of people actually, proud of the players, and they deserve a lot of credit for pulling through that in a tough situation.

"And for the supporters, you know, to be there, they were desperate for us to give them something they could get their teeth into.

"I think it is really important for the players to know what this place can do.

"I am not getting too carried away with things, but it is an important night."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

On the impact of Shea Lacey with his assist for the winning goal:

"Again, not going too over the top, but at the same time, absolutely delighted for Shea. We love him to bits. He is a great young man.

"He is desperate to do well, he has got great ability, so in terms of coming inside and finding a pass, that is not surprising actually, he has got that little glint in his eyes, he plays with a bit of mischief if you like.

"So it is always lovely to have that, but I was just as happy seeing him defending as a right-back when we needed that. I was just as pleased to see him do that on the defensive side.

"I think he gave everybody a bit of a lift coming on the pitch and it was fantastic to see."

#836. Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache

Jack Grealish will do well to get back into the Everton starting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.

Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against opponents who ended with 10 men after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.

And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.

Moyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game following a breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”

Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”

Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”

Newcastle fans had made their feelings about the 3-1 Carabao Cup defeat away to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.

Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.

Frustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.

Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.

Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.

Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

By now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.

Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.

Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.

The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.

“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.

#834. Fernandes claims players don't need to save Carrick's job, but did they?

Bruno Fernandes feels Manchester United players didn't need to save Michael Carrick's job in their 3-2 comeback win over Roma; Carrick's side avoided going ten games without a win for the first time in over four decades

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has come out in support of head coach Michael Carrick, but reiterated that the players didn't need to save his job in their 3-2 comeback win against Roma.

United and Carrick looked dead and buried within the first 18 minutes as the Italian side took a two-goal lead in the early exchanges.

It prompted boos and protests from supporters, who threw tennis balls onto the pitch, but the Red Devils turned things around as a Fernandes penalty and a late Matheus Cunha double gave them their first win in 54 days.

The spirit shown in the performance suggested at least some on-pitch support for Carrick, whose tenure appeared to have been hanging on by a thread ever since the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth.

Fernandes was named on the bench for that game after publicly questioning the tactics in a sobering 4-1 defeat to Como four days prior. His words after Roma, though, were a lot more defiant than accusatory.

"We don't need to save anyone's job," Fernandes told Amazon Prime post-match.

"We've been working so hard to get out of this situation altogether. It's been tough. There's been a lot of speculation in the media, a lot of lies around many things that have happened in this club. Between me and the manager, that we had to clear the air. Nothing like that happened.

"The manager took a decision of putting myself on the bench because I wasn't performing at that level. Everyone felt that it was a punishment for the words that I had. If it was, it was right.

"The manager is the one who makes the decisions. I have to accept them, I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, in the staff and every player that is in this club. It doesn't change my aim to win every game that I have ahead of me. It should be [a turning point]."

Carrick himself similarly played down suggestions that the turnaround could've helped his cause, saying "it's a win for us as a football club," when asked how the result could change the narrative.

"I think we've shown a lot of character as a group to weather what we've had to. You find out a lot about each other, the players will find out things about me. I certainly do about them and their character and what it means to them and what they're prepared to put in."

The win, and the nature of it, feels very reminiscent of a 2018 3-2 win over Newcastle during Jose Mourinho's time at the club. Two early goals stunned the home side, who were already under immense pressure for their poor start to the season.

In the second half, a response. A player who reportedly had his issues with Mourinho, Anthony Martial, found the net en route to a comeback which was secured by a severely underperforming South American in Alexis Sanchez.

Tonight, the role of Mourinho was played by Carrick. The role of Martial you could argue was played by Fernandes, regardless of how he feels his comments following Como were perceived. And the role of Sanchez was bettered by Cunha's heroics.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Did it save Mourinho his job? Ultimately, it didn't. He was sacked by December that year, but maybe it gave him a bit more time at the helm.

In the ten games prior to the Newcastle win, Mourinho's United had only won three times. In the 13 after, they picked up five, plus draws against Chelsea and Arsenal that weren't to be scoffed at. The issue was, the expectations at United were higher in 2018, and that return wasn't cutting it.

In reality, if Carrick managed a run of five wins, four draws and four defeats over the next 13 games, he probably isn't shown the door and is given more time to build on the project. Especially if there are some disagreements from the higher-ups on who should be the man to replace him if they went down that route.

There is just one variable that will make or break things for Carrick. Can he go back-to-back? If his United side can beat Aston Villa on Sunday, it could be the statement the former midfielder needs to earn him more time.

Unai Emery is widely regarded as the best boss in the Premier League. If Carrick is sacked, many United fans would be begging to see him take the hot seat. But, with the spirit and belief in the dressing room higher than it has been in two months following Tuesday's spectacular comeback, Carrick has a chance to get one over on Emery and leave a final impression on his bosses before the international break.

It won't be until Sunday evening, when the final whistle is blown at Old Trafford, that we will truly know whether or not Carrick's men saved his job, rather appropriately, in Fergie time.

#833. Fifa to share documents on World Cup sell-off plans with council members

Viewings to take place at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich

No direct response to Uefa’s questions on governance

Fifa will grant its council members access to documents regarding the doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme but has not responded directly to more than 50 questions from Uefa about its governance and recent scandals.

In a letter sent to the Fifa Council by Mattias Grafström, the governing body’s secretary general, members were told material relating to FFE will be released for them to view in person at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich. They will be allowed only to view the documents, of which the exact nature and scope are unclear, under strict confidentiality protocols. A deadline of 16 November has been set to apply for such visits; eyebrows may be raised in some quarters about the fact this is two days before candidates for the Fifa election next year are required to declare their hand.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Uefa had written to Grafström on 19 October giving Fifa a fortnight to answer a series of questions about FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair, the Fifa peace prize, the organisation’s relations with Donald Trump and other major decisions that have caused controversy in the past 12 months. It had asked for all documents regarding FFE to be made accessible, saying refusal to comply with any of its demands should be “justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon”.

The deadline imposed by Uefa expired on Monday night, although Fifa Council members are understood to have been told a response is being worked upon and will be shared with them. Fifa’s stance is that Uefa’s questions, posed after Gianni Infantino told delegates at the Fifa Council meeting last month to submit questions in writing before they next convened in December, were too substantial in number for the two-week turnaround.

It remains to be seen whether those Fifa Council members who travel for the document inspection will depart with the answers they require. In August Uefa made an application to four courts in the US for the release of documents pertaining to FFE, with a view to lodging a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement. Preliminary rulings are yet to be handed down and the amount of information available to view may be affected. Fifa has accused Uefa of “harassment” and “misinformation” and denied wrongdoing by Infantino.

As reported last week Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate who could stand against Infantino in March, with movement possible early this month.

#831. AFC postpones Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia to late 2027 due to conflict in Middle East

Tournament pushed back 11 months with proposed start on 23 December

New dates with 21 January 2028 final must be approved by Fifa

The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed as a result of the conflict in the Middle East.

After a month of speculation following the airport attack on Riyadh’s international airport, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) confirmed on Tuesday that the tournament had been pushed back 11 months.

The rescheduled tournament is expected to kick off in the 2027 Christmas break with a 23 December start date leading up to a 21 January 2028 final.

“The organising committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions,” the AFC said in a statement.

“Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.”

The proposed new dates – which fall in one of the busiest periods in European club football – must be approved by Fifa.

Saudi Arabia’s suitability to host the tournament has been a hot topic since the Riyadh airport attack by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Other nations, who were scheduled to travel to Saudi Arabia in the November international window, have been forced to relocate their friendlies.

There was little appetite for another host nation to step in at such short notice – the tournament was slated to start on 7 January 2027 – but going ahead as planned in the current climate was fraught with risks.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

In Australia, the delayed tournament could have ramifications for coach Tony Popovic, who signed a short-term extension on the eve of the World Cup.

Popovic’s contract is due to expire after the previously scheduled January tournament, where Australia were due to face Tajikistan, Singapore and Iraq, who are coached by ex-Socceroos boss Graham Arnold.

Arnold was handed a job reprieve by the Iraqi FA last month after a form slump following the country’s first World Cup qualification in 40 years.

#829. Serbia: Hope, tension and apprehension as voters prepare to elect new parliament

After two years of protests, Serbia faces a pivotal election on Sunday, with a student-led challenge to Aleksandar Vucic's lengthy rule. Allegations of electoral irregularities and fears of a post-election crisis abound.

A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years.

The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination.

"We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd.

"People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List.

After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power.

For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign.

"These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote."

The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure.

In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics.

Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally.

The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos.

The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests.

"They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements."

The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies.

By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners.

CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance  and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters.

In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks.

Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government.

But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome.

He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports.

There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters.

Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative.

Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party.

DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party.

Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety.

For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night.

The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result.

"But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally.

Whatever happens, the European Union's response could be crucial.

"I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW.

An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012.

Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo, a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box.

But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed.

#827. Phil Foden sets sights on England recall and says he has had no contact with Tuchel

Foden: ‘You have to keep putting on performances’

Enzo Maresca: ‘We cannot rely on Erling for every game’

Phil Foden is aiming for an England recall after the Manchester City attacker was left out of the squad for last summer’s World Cup and the Nations League games this season by Thomas Tuchel.

While the next round of England games in the competition – the squad for which will be named on Friday – may come too soon for a recall, Foden wants to force his way back into Tuchel’s plans. The 26-year-old said: “Hopefully, one day the call-up might come back. It’s one of those things [being dropped]. Football is full of ups and downs. You have to try your best, keep putting on performances.”

Foden revealed Tuchel has not been in touch since the World Cup to discuss what the manager wishes to see from him. “No, I haven’t really spoken to him to be honest, so not much to say on that,” he said.

In September’s 1-0 win at Manchester United Foden was sent off after 23 minutes, resulting in a three-match ban. As this came a week before the last international window, he did not play again for more than a month.

Foden said: “Obviously, I had the unfortunate red against United but the break did me good, I came back fresh and sharp. I’ve been involved in a lot of goals recently and I’m happy. Personally [the season] – it’s gone really well. I took some family time [after the red card], went on holiday. It was a very long time, which felt strange. It gave me time to work on things I need to work on. I felt like I could help the team.”

Before City face RB Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday, Enzo Maresca conceded that City cannot rely on Erling Haaland to score in every game, with the manager clear that more support is needed from the rest of the squad.

Saturday’s 1-0 loss to Brighton was the first time Maresca’s side has failed to score this season. Yet despite racking up 36 goals in all competitions, Haaland’s 13 is seven more than the next highest scorer, Rayan Cherki. Foden’s four goals – including a hat-trick in City’s last European outing, against AEK Athens – is the third best.

Maresca said: “It’s very important that in each game we create chances. For sure when you have Erling inside the pitch, it’s better because he’s going to score goals. But you know that he’s always there, close. At the same time, we cannot rely on Erling for every game.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“We need the rest to score goals. But I think the last game against Brighton was the only game of the season where we didn’t score. If Erling is on the pitch, we are happy. But also we need the rest to score goals.”

In the 2023-24 season Foden scored 27 goals, a career high. He was asked if he can support Haaland more and produce his form of three years ago. “Hopefully,” he said. “[The key is] keep playing regularly, being happy and positive. Being in the right positions and hopefully I can get back to that level now. I’m getting there slightly more now.”

#825. Chinese doctoral students in clinical medicine can graduate without a thesis — more degrees to follow

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Postgraduate students studying clinical medicine in China have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case, rather than a thesis.Credit: Xie Shangguo/VCG via Getty

Master’s and doctoral candidates in some clinical medicine degrees in China can now graduate with a ‘practical achievement’ instead of a thesis. This is the second field to open such a pathway. Since 2024, master’s and PhD students in engineering have been allowed to graduate from universities across China after developing a new product, technique, project or installation.

On 22 October, a team of government-appointed education advisers released draft policy documents setting out the rules for the graduation pathway for students pursuing a professional master’s or doctoral degree in clinical medicine — both are three-year courses typically taken by medical graduates and practising physicians.

In China, professional postgraduate courses focus on training students to solve problems in a particular line of work rather than developing research skills, as they would in an academic degree. The rules state that students have the option to graduate with a practical achievement, such as an analysis of a special clinical case or an investigation into a problem facing medical institutes.

Postgraduate courses in translation, agriculture, accounting and arts are expected to introduce similar pathways to graduation, according to China’s Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council, a government body driving reforms for postgraduate education.

These reforms are a step in the right direction, because students preparing for professional careers should be trained and assessed in ways that reflect those careers, says Futao Huang, a researcher of higher-education policy at Hiroshima University in Higashihiroshima, Japan. “The real challenge is to develop credible, transparent and profession-specific standards for assessing practical achievements,” Huang adds.

For students pursuing a professional degree in clinical medicine, the new graduation pathway means that they can be assessed on the contribution that their research will bring to patients and society, says Zhou Feifei, a spinal surgeon at Peking University Third Hospital in Beijing. “This will encourage them to find problems in real life and to address the problem using a scientific way,” he adds.

One of Zhou’s students, Tie Dazhao, was the first person to graduate with a ‘practical PhD’ in clinical medicine in June, having been selected as a pilot case in 2023. Tie developed an artificial-intelligence-empowered software programme that can help physicians to classify a type of rare spinal condition and recommend suitable treatment strategies to them, says Zhou.

Individual universities are encouraged to form their own policies on training practical postgraduate students and what requirements students must meet to graduate, says Liping Duan, chief physician of gastroenterology at Peking University Third Hospital and a member of a national advisory committee tasked with formulating the policy for clinical medicine. One of the biggest challenges will be creating a uniform standard to assess practical achievements, Duan says. “What works for cardiology may not work for dermatology, for example,” she adds.

How to control the quality of the achievements will also be important, Duan says. “Some people may mistakenly think that graduation has become easier now that students can choose not to write a thesis.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03480-7

Correction 03 November 2026: A previous version of this story used PhD students instead of doctoral students.

#821. Wrexham suffer 'significant' Smith injury blow

Sam Smith joined Wrexham from Reading in January 2025

Wrexham forward Sam Smith is facing a "significant" spell out of action due to a knee injury, manager Phil Parkinson has confirmed.

Smith suffered the injury during Wrexham's 1-0 defeat at Sheffield United in the Championship on Friday.

The 28-year-old will see a specialist later on Tuesday to discover the extent of the damage and the duration of his absence.

"Unfortunately for... it looks like he's going to face a significant period on the sidelines," Parkinson said.

"He came off against Sheffield and went back and carried on and his knee swelled up significantly the next day.

"He sees a specialist this afternoon (Tuesday) and we will know more then.

"Our initial thoughts are that he could need surgery, but we'll know more after today."

Smith's injury is a further blow to Parkinson and his team before they host Championship leaders Middlesbrough on Wednesday (19:45 GMT).

Forwards Josh Windass and Nathan Broadhead are still sidelined while Callum O'Hare remains a doubt after missing the loss at Bramall Lane.

Parkinson said their absence presents an opportunity for others including youngster Bailey Cadamarteri, the Jamaica international.

The 21-year-old, who joined from Sheffield Wednesday in January, has yet to start a senior game for the Dragons with his five appearances this season coming off the bench.

"That's what happens in football clubs, people come out of the side and other people say, 'this is my chance to step up to the plate and show what I'm all about'," Parkinson added.

"Undoubtedly Bailey's going to get some game time and I'm looking forward to seeing that.

"Bailey's ready and chomping at the bit and with Sam's injury he's going to get an opportunity and more game time.

#819. Mee and Kenny handed first Northern Ireland call-ups

Dermot Mee and Eoin Kenny are both underage internationals with Northern Ireland

Manchester United goalkeeper Dermot Mee and Portsmouth forward Eoin Kenny have been handed their first Northern Ireland call-ups for November's final Nations League matches with Ukraine and Hungary.

Mee, 23, is a former Northern Ireland underage international and, although he has not played competitively for United this season, will add competition to NI's first choice goalkeeper Pierce Charles.

"He's been on [Under-]21s in the past so he knows a lot of the players," said manager Michael O'Neill.

"He's currently third-choice at Manchester United, he's involved obviously in their Champions League squads and I had a good chat with Jonny Evans about him. He spoke very highly of him."

Attacker Kenny, who is the son of former Republic of Ireland manager Stephen, joined Portsmouth from Dundalk in July.

The 20-year-old has made one league appearance for the Championship club, but has been handed a first call after impressing for the Northern Ireland Under-21s under Tommy Wright.

"I think this is really a reward for a strong campaign for Tommy in the 21s," added O'Neill.

"He made that move from from Dundalk to Portsmouth in the summer and it just gives us a chance to see him."

Striker Dion Charles and goalkeeper Bailey Peacock-Farrell drop out of the squad.

Sunderland defender Dan Ballard is missing after he injured his hamstring in the September win over Georgia in Tbilisi, while defender Eoin Toal, midfielders Ali McCann and Jamie McDonnell are also absent through injury.

Liverpool's Conor Bradley, who has not played since January, remains a long-term absentee.

Family affair at Croke Park caps Mee's special night

Michael O'Neill's side are unbeaten at the top of League B2 and can earn promotion to the top tier for the first time.

Northern Ireland face Ukraine at Windsor Park on Saturday, 14 November at 19:45 GMT before they travel to Hungary in their final match on 17 November.

Both games are live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sounds.

The average of Northern Ireland's squad is just 23.5, and 17 of the 25 players selected are aged 23 or under.

O'Neill admitted he would rather have the likes of the injured Ballard, Bradley, McCann and Toal available, but he knows the window will be important in building depth in the squad.

"I think that the squad has to continue to develop players, they have to step in and you have to give players the opportunity to do that," he said.

"It's a very young squad and it will be stretched again. We'll be tested in these two games, but we given ourselves a good chance with obviously what we've done to date in the games."

Northern Ireland are the only side left in the entire Nations League who have yet to concede a goal in this year's competition.

Shea Charles scored a last-gasp winner in Georgia in September before a goalless draw at home to Hungary.

A 3-0 victory over Ukraine was one of the most impressive performances from O'Neill's young side, and they ended the quadruple-header with another goalless draw, this time at home to Georgia.

If Northern Ireland can top the group they would not only win promotion to League A, but they would also be all but guaranteed of a play-off for Euro 2028.

#818. Newcastle and Palace progress in EFL Trophy

Kyran Thompson's winner for Newcastle Under-21s came in the 34th minute

Newcastle United and Crystal Palace's under-21 sides both secured passage to the knockout stages of the Jersey Mike's Trophy with narrow wins at League Two clubs.

Kyran Thompson's goal earned Newcastle's youngsters a 1-0 victory at Rotherham United in Northern Group C to eliminate the Millers and ensured the Magpies will progress along with leaders Bradford City.

David Angibeaud's winner gave Palace a 2-1 win at Newport County in Southern Group E, with the Premier League side now guaranteed to progress alongside Plymouth Argyle.

There was no such luck for Brighton & Hove Albion U21, however, as they were thrashed 6-0 at League One side Cambridge United in Southern Group G.

Over-age Seagulls player Ben Barclay did not set a good example for his younger team-mates as the 30-year-old was sent off for deliberate handball in the first half.

Isaac Heath scored the resulting penalty and Cambridge fully capitalised on the numerical advantage by scoring five more times in the ensuing half-hour.

Callum Stead notched twice as the U's claimed a third win in three games in the competition to clinch top spot in the group and end Brighton's hopes in the process.

In Tuesday's other game, Doncaster Rovers won 4-1 at Rochdale in Northern Group H to eliminate both their hosts and Liverpool U21, who can now finish no higher than third in the pool.

#816. Detroit Lions Coach Shares Update on Jack Campbell After Neck Injury

After Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell suffered a major neck injury during the team’s game against the Minnesota Vikings, coach Dan Campbell shared an update on his recovery.

Days after the Detroit Lions linebacker suffered a neck injury in his team’s match-up against the Minnesota Vikings Nov. 1, his coach Dan Campbell shared an update.

“It’s not easy because he’s going to always be on our minds over here,” Dan, who shares no relation to his player, said while phoning into the 97.1 The Ticket Radio Show Nov. 3. “The good news is he is improving.”

The NFL coach—who has been with the Lions for five seasons—also shared an update on his player during a press conference for his team Nov. 2.

“It’s positive,” he said at the time. “Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We'll leave it at that, so continue to pray for him. But it is positive.”

Despite the Lions' 19-15 win against the Vikings Nov. 1, the team’s success was overshadowed by Jack’s terrifying injury, which occurred during the fourth quarter.

In footage from the game, Jack—who welcomed son Cooper with wife Megan Campbell in July—can be seen lying face down on the field, seemingly unable to move after tackling Vikings player T.J. Hockenson. The 26-year-old was quickly approached by medical personnel before being lifted off the field on a backboard.

Following the game, the Lions shared an update on the football player to X, writing in a post, “Jack Campbell is being transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury.”

As of the evening of Nov. 2, the University of Iowa alum remained hospitalized.

“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the Lions wrote in a separate post on their X account Nov. 2. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”

While addressing Jack’s injury, Dan emphasized the value that the player—who has played for the team since he was drafted in 2023 and was tapped as captain earlier this year—brings to the team.

“I don’t even know if I can put it into words,” Dan said during a press conference Nov. 2. “You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys that has been assembled. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy, he’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back. He’s just all heart, man. All effort.”

The 50-year-old emphasized that Jack is “an unbelievable person.”

“Down to Earth,” he continued. “Very genuine. There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him.”

For a deeper look into Campbell's injury and recovery, keep reading…

Jack Campbell was injured during the Detroit Lions’ Nov. 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings

In the fourth quarter of the teams' match-up, Campbell tackled opponent T.J. Hockenson—his third tackle of the game—and was hit on the way down.

He lay face-down on the field, unable to move after the play, and had to be carried off on a backboard by medical personnel.

Campbell was rushed to a nearby hospital to have his neck evaluated

A reporter present at the game called Campbell’s hit the “scariest moment” he’d ever witnessed at Ford Field in a Nov. 1 post on X. He also confirmed that Campbell’s wife Megan Campbell and their baby boy Cooper, who was born in July 2026, were brought down to the field to accompany the player in an ambulance.

Lions coach Dan Campbell—who has no relation to the linebacker—said the team was “thinking about him” in a post-game interview, but had no information to share.

In a post on X following the game, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was brought “to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury.”

Campbell has remained hospitalized following his injury

On Nov. 2, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was being closely monitored at the hospital.

“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the team wrote in a post on X. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”

Lions coach says Campbell’s recovery update is “positive”

In a press conference one day after Campbell’s injury, Coach Campbell confirmed a heartening update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s positive,” he said. “Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We’ll leave it at that. Just continue to pray for him but it is positive news on Jack.”

Coach Campbell calls player an “unbelievable person”

While addressing his player’s injury, the Detroit Lions coach emphasized Campbell’s impact on the team, especially after he was tapped as team captain for this season.

“I don’t even know if I can put it into words,” Dan said during a press conference Nov. 2. “You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys that has been assembled. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy, he’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back. He’s just all heart, man. All effort."

As he put it, “There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him,”

In an appearance on 97.1 The Ticket Radio Show Nov. 3, Coach Campbell shared an update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s not easy because he’s going to always be on our minds over here,” he said. “The good news is he is improving.”

#815. How to follow the Champions League on the BBC

Paris St-Germain are the holders of the Champions League

The Champions League returns this week - and you can watch highlights of Europe's showpiece club competition on the BBC throughout this season.

Aston Villa and Liverpool are the best-performing English clubs in the 2026-27 league phase so far, winning three games from three to put them level at the top on points with Paris Saint-Germain, Real Madrid and Real Betis.

Just like the previous two seasons, from 22:00 BST on the Wednesday of Champions League matchweeks, there will be game-by-game highlights available on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app.

You'll also be able to watch highlights - along with analysis from our experts on the big stories and talking points - on Match of the Day on Wednesdays on BBC One at 22:40 (this week at 23:10 in Wales, 23:40 in Northern Ireland).

There will be clips available on the BBC Sport website, app and on social media.

You will also be able to follow all the action online and on the BBC Sport app through our live text coverage, as well as listen to radio commentary.

BBC Radio 5 Live will continue to have live commentary of selected Champions League games and you can also listen on the BBC Sounds app and your smart speaker.

BBC podcasts Football Daily and Euro Leagues will bring you reaction and the biggest talking points from the Champions League throughout the campaign.

This year's competition includes five British clubs: Arsenal, Aston Villa, Liverpool, Manchester City and Manchester United.

It means the BBC has highlights of the Premier League, Champions League and FA Cup this season.

TNT Sport and Amazon Prime Video will show Champions League games live in the UK.

Amazon have first pick of the Tuesday games - 17 matches in total - with all of the other matches shown on TNT.
