#802. Kenny's background 'not that important' to O'Neill

Eoin Kenny's father, Stephen Kenny, managed the Republic of Ireland for three years between 2020 and 2023

Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill said new call-up Eoin Kenny's family connection to the Republic of Ireland is not something he considered before bringing him into the senior squad for this month's Nations League fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary.

The Portsmouth player, who joined the Championship side from Dundalk in the summer transfer window, is the son of former Republic of Ireland manager Stephen Kenny.

A 20-year-old attacker, Eoin Kenny was born in Northern Ireland while his father was manager of Derry City but represented Republic of Ireland at under-19 level.

He switched to Northern Ireland to play under-21s, turning out 11 times for Tommy Wright's side and captaining them against Greece last month.

"The background is not really that important for me, if I'm honest. I just look at the lad as a player," said O'Neill.

"He's really enjoyed being in the Northern Ireland set-up and, I think off the back of a really strong under-21s campaign, he deserves the opportunity to be in the squad."

The former Stoke City boss added: "I would envisage that he's here because he wants to be here. The most important thing is that he has the chance to play international football."

Live coverage of Northern Ireland's Nations League fixtures at home to Ukraine (14 November) and away to Hungary (17 November) will be available on BBC TV, BBC iPlayer, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport NI website.

While Stephen Kenny was named Republic of Ireland manager the same month - April 2020 - that Michael O'Neill ended his first stint as Northern Ireland boss, the pair had previously cross paths in the League of Ireland.

O'Neill, however, said he did not speak to Stephen Kenny before the call-up, but took on board the recommendation of Northern Ireland under-21 manager Tommy Wright.

"It wasn't me that brought him in, it was Tommy Wright that brought him in initially and so he's been around it," said O'Neill of Kenny's initial return to the Northern Ireland set-up last year.

"I knew of him obviously through Stephen, and that he played in the League of Ireland, but it was only when the eligibility thing came to the forefront and Tommy Wright had him in with the 21s [that he came on to O'Neill's radar].

"Tommy has been very positive about him in terms of his level of performance but also what he is like as a lad as well."

Kenny has made one Championship appearance for Portsmouth with O'Neill believing the upcoming window is a good opportunity to see the player up close, while also showing there is a path from under-21 to senior international football.

"It just gives us a chance to see him really, otherwise we're waiting on him getting minutes at Portsmouth.

"He's had some, but it's not been easy for him in terms of getting minutes. He's made a positive impact since he went there, but you never see the players truly until you get them in and get the chance to work with them. That was the rationale.

"I think it's important that the 21s players see that there is a pathway for them because too often for a lot of players their international careers stopped at 21s."

The issue of international allegiance has again been an increasingly hot topic in the build-up to recent internationals, centred around young Arsenal forward Ceadach O'Neill.

The promising 18-year-old won his fourth cap for Northern Ireland against Georgia in the Nations League last month, tying him permanently to the side despite an attempt by the Republic of Ireland to encourage an international transfer.

After Northern Ireland under-21 international Conor Haughey hit the winning penalty in Fleetwood Town's shock win over Arsenal in the EFL Cup last week - when Ceadach O'Neill made his debut for the Gunners - he became the latest subject of similar speculation.

O'Neill, however, said he has not felt the need to discuss the issue with the 19-year-old defender.

"We've no need to have those conversations," he said.

"At the end of the day, he's part of our under-21 group and he's on the radar of the senior squad.

"We don't have those conversations until it comes to the point that the player indicates that he would want to make an international transfer and we're not at that point."

O'Neill was at Highbury to witness Haughey's headline-grabbing moment last week and was impressed by the centre-back's display even before the penalty heroics.

"I normally would leave a game just before the end, but I stayed to the end in this case and stayed for the penalties," he added.

"I was a little bit surprised to see Conor step up and take the fifth penalty, but it showed real confidence which is nice to see in a young player. It showed a really positive attitude.

"I felt he played well in the game, that was more important for me. He's playing against [Viktor] Gyokeres, he's playing against [Kai] Havertz, so to get through the game and take it to penalties was a big achievement for Fleetwood and big for a young player to be involved in that type of game."

#801. How democracy depends on science — and must protect it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Martin Kahanec is a professor at the Central European University, Vienna, Austria, and affiliated with the Central European Labor Studies Institute and Bratislava University of Economics and Business, Bratislava, Slovakia, and the European University Institute, Florence, Italy.

Naomi Ellemers is a distinguished professor at Utrecht University, Utrecht, the Netherlands.

Adam Izdebski is a professor of human ecology at the Institute of Advanced Studies, Nicolaus Copernicus University, Toruń, Poland.

Rafal M. Łukasik is a professor of chemical engineering and the director of the Łukasiewicz Research Network, Industrial Chemistry Institute, Warsaw, Poland.

Dimitra Simeonidou is a professor of high-performance networks and the director of the Smart Internet Lab at the University of Bristol, Bristol, UK.

Rémy Slama is a senior investigator and professor at INSERM and ENS-PSL, Paris, France.

Mangala Srinivas is a professor of cell biology and immunology at Wageningen University and Research, Wageningen, the Netherlands.

For scientists, thoughts about democracy can feel distant from their work. Yet, around the world, governments are limiting academic freedom and interfering with decisions about what research is funded and who performs it1. Some scientists are also facing politically motivated interference and attacks2.

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

As members of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, we feel it is urgent to address this concern and that we have a responsibility to make scientists’ voices heard.

Science and democracy are often viewed as distinct — science as a source of discovery, expertise and innovation and democracy as a set of institutions, rules and procedures. But, in reality, the two are intertwined3.

Science is an essential backbone of democracy. In an increasingly complex and fast-changing world, people need access to verified information and independent knowledge to make informed decisions4,5. Research aids that by generating reliable evidence and fostering critical enquiry, thus enabling a plurality of views to be discussed and creating conditions in which societies can learn from experience.

In May, Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, asked us to provide advice on how science can strengthen the European Union’s democratic functioning and resilience.

Independently of that process, here we put forward three pillars through which science enables democracy: establishing shared factual baselines, aiding trust in institutions and providing tools to adapt policies and organizations in response to changing circumstances.

The first pillar relates to protecting the foundations and integrity of information on which democratic judgements, collective deliberation and, ultimately, action depend.

Democratic societies constantly confront questions for which there are no simple, best or permanent answers. Scientific institutions help societies to navigate changing realities by creating procedures for gathering evidence about the current situation, past trends, probable outcomes or management options; assessing impacts; communicating disagreement; quantifying uncertainties; and updating conclusions in light of new findings.

Artificial-intelligence and other digital platforms are changing how people find information, develop opinions and take part in public life6. This not only provides opportunities for broadening participation and increasing transparency, but also produces intensified, increasingly complex or fresh risks, including of misinformation, manipulation, bias, polarization and fragmentation6,7. Moreover, these developments amplify the disproportionate influence of a small number of powerful technology companies and their leaders8, including their ability to ‘manufacture doubt’ and shape public opinion9,10.

How to get science back into policymaking

How to get science back into policymaking

The challenge goes further than just correcting people’s misconceptions. Disinformation is often rooted in social networks, reinforced by emotions and group identities and used deliberately for political purposes5,7. It spreads through networks of people connected by identity, grievance or distrust. These vulnerabilities can be exploited by individuals seeking to advance political or economic interests9, thereby undermining democratic institutions, deepening divisions and fostering instability6.

Citizens have legitimate concerns about economic restructuring, regional inequities, how migration is governed, technological changes, ageing populations, climate risks and geopolitical instability. People might lose trust in democratic institutions, especially if they feel they are not being heard, do not understand why something changed, think they are treated unfairly or see the fabric of their communities being disrupted11. This might create vulnerabilities that can be exploited through disinformation and political manipulation5.

For this reason, scientific approaches to democratic resilience must go beyond fact-checking and include the design of effective channels for science communication and information sharing, as well as opportunities for meaningful public participation and informed deliberation4,12. These should include transparent data sources in digital platforms; independent media; strong safeguards against foreign interference; secure information infrastructures; independent monitoring and assurance of algorithmic systems; and improved understanding of how the expanding use of AI tools might shape democratic discourse and outcomes13.

The second pillar refers to the legitimacy of expertise and the trustworthiness of institutions. Democratic governance can be thought of as a shared societal capacity to understand complex realities, to deliberate across differences and to act together in the face of social, economic and technological transformations and uncertainty4,6. Its resilience rests on organizations that sustain public trust and active citizenship, and on people’s capacity to participate meaningfully in deliberation and collective problem-solving4,14.

Institutions that are informed by scientific evidence and guided by scientific principles are better equipped than others to make effective, transparent and accountable decisions, strengthening public trust in democracy11. During a pandemic or other crisis, or in anticipation of such events, authorities can reinforce trust by explaining clearly how scientific evidence, including any limitations and uncertainties, informs their decisions.

But for science to strengthen democracy, researchers must be trusted, too15,16. Moreover, the legitimacy of expertise has become increasingly contested over the past few years in Europe and elsewhere5,15.

Scientific advice is subjected to politicization in many countries, with consensual insights and clear evidence (such as on climate change) being dismissed as ‘just another opinion’ or as being driven by a political agenda5,9. Public trust in expertise has become polarized along political lines5,15. Some officials and politicians might support specific strands of science, for instance, by promoting individual researchers or a few disciplines selectively. Such favouritism has implications for funding.

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

This ‘divide and rule’ approach to science is often tacitly accepted by the academic community, with many institutions preferring to stay silent rather than run the risk of their budgets being cut. The dilution of scientific knowledge in an ever-increasing flow of online information, often promoted by individuals with vested interests seeking to influence public decisions, can also render impartial scientific evidence and advice less visible.

Expertise strengthens democratic legitimacy when it is transparent, diverse, independent and open to scrutiny — as prescribed by the rules of science. But it weakens legitimacy when it is perceived as opaque, unclear, politicized, elitist or disconnected from people’s lived experiences.

Ensuring that expert information is democratically legitimate requires institutions and mechanisms that not only structure the interaction between science, policy and society, but also protect organizations’ separate, independent roles, manage conflicts of interests and prevent undue influence.

Crucially, not every engagement with science carries equal weight. Impartial access to scientific knowledge is most reliably secured through a cross-disciplinary and diverse group of experts. By contrast, the opinion of a single scientist might result in partial understanding (highlighting a particular disciplinary perspective) or reliance on a dissenting voice that differs from the majority view. High-level expert groups, which engage directly with senior decision makers, can identify a broader range of potential concerns. They can better understand the wider implications of policy challenges to provide relevant scientific evidence and advice, yet maintain independence in their analysis, conclusions and recommendations.

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Public institutions should ensure that scientists who provide advice can do so independently and that they are free to publish their findings. This generally requires stable public funding of research1. Cuts to public science budgets can increase scientists’ dependence on a narrow range of funders, including private and commercial organizations or institutions linked to other countries. Their funding decisions could reflect strategic or political interests and might create actual or perceived conflicts of interest if appropriate transparency guidelines and safeguards are not in place.

The European Commission’s science-advice framework provides a useful example of how scientific independence can be achieved. It combines topic-specific evidence reviews by multidisciplinary expert groups with independent policy recommendations from its seven chief scientific advisers. The advisers are supported by a permanent secretariat that helps them to align scientific advice with policy needs and safeguards the independence of the advisory process. This mechanism also includes rules on transparency and the disclosure of advisers’ conflicts of interest (see go.nature.com/4jndrg).

Scientific expert groups should be able to propose topics, identify questions and communicate evidence, uncertainties and policy options to decision makers and the public independently.

But trust depends on people having the opportunity to engage with science, too. Scientific literacy, civic education, public engagement with research and access to reliable information are all essential and need to be supported by public and educational institutions. Opportunities for science education are a public good and should be accessible to all.

#800. A Fresh Look at Exes Will Smith and Sheree Zampino's Co-Parenting Bond

While Will Smith and Sheree Zampino got hitched and then divorced in the 90s, they've remained on good terms. See how they've continued their pursuit of happiness as co-parents.

Now this is a story all about how Will Smith and Sheree Zampino’s life got flipped, turned upside down.

And we'd like to take a minute, just sit right there, to tell you how The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum and the Hollywood Exes star went from married, to divorced, to co-parents who’ve remained on good terms. So good, in fact, that Smith and Zampino were recently spotted sharing a few laughs at the airport in Sydney, Australia, where he’d been filming his new movie Supermax.

Not that this is super shocking. After all, Smith’s wife Jada Pinkett Smith has noted that he and Zampino still go on trips together—not in a romantic way but in the sense that they’re still family as parents to 33-year-old son Trey.

"She and Will have their own relationship," the Girls Trip actress said on Sway’s Universe in 2018. "She’s gone on vacations with Will without me with Trey. Because I feel as though Trey needs to feel that dynamic between his two parents. That’s very important that he can feel that connection and where they do meet."

As for how they first met, it was back in the early 90s when Smith attended a taping of Different World. While the Men in Black star’s mission had originally been to impress Pinkett Smith, he ended up meeting Zampino.

"I didn’t meet Jada that night," he recalled in his 2021 memoir Will. "Sheree and I left together before the show was even over. We laughed all the way through dinner, all the way through that fall, and three months later, we were married."

Getting hitched in 1992, Smith and Zampino welcomed Trey later that year. And as their family grew, so did the actor’s career—with him landing the role in 1993’s Six Degrees of Separation shortly after they wed.

But ultimately, Smith and Zampino realized their pursuit of happiness wasn’t with each other. And on Valentine’s Day 1995, she filed for divorce.

Noting they tied the knot in their early 20s, "Marriage is not easy, especially at that age," Zampino said in a 2016 social media video. “Now, we’re trying to be parents, navigate through our marriage, I couldn’t reconcile all of that. Will was becoming bigger and bigger with his career. I’m becoming smaller and smaller and smaller. I didn’t have the tools. We didn’t have the tools to make it work. I left because I was unhappy. It’s really that simple.”

And Smith has been honest about the challenges he faced following their divorce.

"With Sheree and with Trey, that was a really difficult time," the Oscar winner noted on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2020. "Divorce was the worst thing in my adult life. Divorce was the ultimate failure for me. I’ve been hurt a lot in my adult life, but I don’t think anything touches the failure of getting divorced from my 2-year-old son’s mother."

Smith went on to marry Pinkett Smith in 1997. They welcomed son Jaden the next year followed by daughter Willow in 2000. And along with Zampino and Trey, they learned how to become a blended family.

"We really had to figure it out along the way," Pinkett Smith shared on Red Table Talk in 2018. "For me, it really was just about maturity. Just not understanding the marital dynamic like, 'OK, well, divorce papers are sent, and people are over it, then this is done.' Guess what? It aint never done."

Because as she put it, "This woman is a part of this family. It’s not only taking on Trey, but Sheree was coming along too. It’s part of the package."

"There were times where we have bumped heads and it hasn't been pretty," Zampino admitted on Behind the Velvet Rope in 2022. “But listen, we get back on that horse and we press on. We do what we have to do. Because again, at the end of the day, it's about the kids. We have a responsibility to them."

And they have a desire to support each other too. Like how Zampino was the first guest on Pinkett Smith’s Red Table Talk and stood in Smith’s corner after he slapped Chris Rock at the 2020 Oscars.

"I hope people allow him to be human," she told DailyMail.com in 2022. "I really hope for that because I stand in support of him, we are on good terms."

Over the years, their family has gone through changes, including Zampino’s marriage and divorce from Terrell Fletcher as well as Smith and Pinkett’s separation.

"We are together," Pinkett Smith clarified on It’s Been a Minute in 2024, "but we are together in the way that works for us."

And it seems that Zampino and Smith will always be tied together too.  "I think that in terms of co-parenting, we’re more successful, a lot more successful actually, than in a marriage dynamic," she told Fox News in 2020. "We were put on this Earth to be co-parents. That’s what we did and that’s what we’re doing. We love each other and it’s been amazing. It’s been a blessing."

So no, Zampino didn’t agree with Smith calling their divorce a failure.

"I had an issue with that because I didn’t understand how we could do what we do as a blended family and do it as well as we do and as loving as we do and have an amazing son, and it’s looked at as a failure," she said on Red Table Talkin 2022. "It did what it was supposed to do, so that was successful."

And they're not the only ones chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool. Keep reading to see more successful celebrity co-parents.

Though the Grammy winner and Swedish-Syrian artist called it quits in 2023, the pair continue to partner when it comes to their kids Lucia and Renn.

“We’ve actually had the most wonderful relationship,” Jwan told Attitude in September 2025. “It’s a very solid and calm co-parenting situation. We live 10 minutes away from each other. We speak every other day. We love our kids so much.”

He added, “It’s been an extremely lovely kind of experience. It’s not an experience—it’s a way of living.”

Megan Fox and Brian Austin Green have a body of co-parenting experience. So the Jennifer’s Body star and the Beverly Hills, 90210 alum—who share kids Noah, Bodhi and Journey—try to follow a key rule. "The number one," Brian told E! News in April 2024, "is always make sure that everything is centered around the experience of the kids." Because as he put it, a breakup is “gonna affect the kids. The only choice you have is how it affects the kids.” Part of that, Brian continued, is recognizing that it’s important to “pick your battles.”"The person that you were with that you're now separated from, you guys are separated for a reason," he added, "because you didn't get along. So, you can't expect to then get along after the fact in raising your kids. So, you have to decide, ‘OK, it's not about us getting along anymore. It's about us co-parenting, which is a totally different situation.'"Megan—whose divorce from Brian was finalized in 2022 two years after the filing—agrees. "I think it's really important when people separate to never ever disparage the other parent or even in a passive aggressive way make remarks," the Transformers actress said on a 2023 episode of The Drew Barrymore Show. "I don't let anything in my energy like that when I'm around my kids. Because if I don't accept and love their father, I'm rejecting a part of them because he's a part of who they are always. He's in their blood, and he's in their psyche, and they exist because of him."

Where is the love? Josh Duhamel and Fergie certainly have it for each other as co-parents."Fergie is an amazing woman. She really is," the Safe Haven actor said on a 2023 episode of The Jess Cagle Show, going on to share how the singer welcomed his wife Audra Mari into the family. "She's taken Audra in. And it could be much worse. That's the thing—you never know how these things are going to go."In fact, Josh said Fergie was thrilled for the couple after they announced in 2023 that they were expecting their first child together: Shepherd. The little one—born in January 2024—joined big brother Axl, whom the Las Vegas alum shares with the former Black Eyed Peas member."Because she's such a kind-hearted person, she really truly is, she only has love for Audra and is excited as—well, I can't believe how excited she is for us," continued Josh—whose divorce from Fergie was finalized in 2019, two years after they announced their split. "Like I said, it could be a lot worse. I've seen it, I've lived it. Thankfully, we have a really civil situation."Along with Axl and Shepherd, Josh shares daughter Rocca de Leon with Audra.

Irina Shayk, who shares daughter Lea with ex Bradley Cooper, isn't a big fan of the terminology.“I never understood the term co-parenting,” the model told ELLE in 2021. “When I’m with my daughter, I’m 100 percent a mother, and when she’s with her dad, he’s 100 percent her dad. Co-parenting is parenting.” Though Irina and Bradley split in 2019 after four years together, they've continued to stay on good terms. And even with their busy schedules, the runway vet and the Silver Linings Playbook actor have continued to go on family vacations, hang out in New York and support one another since their breakup.“He’s the best father Lea and I could dream of," she told the magazine in 2023. "It always works, but it always works because we make it work.”

As Mariah Carey put it, love takes time—and so can finding a rhythm in co-parenting. However, Nick Cannon, who shares twins Moroccan and Monroe with the Grammy winner, suggested they’ve settled into a good routine.“Mariah and I co-parent very well,” The Masked Singer host said on a 2022 episode of The Language of Love with Dr. Laura Berman. “We’re really great friends. She’s taught me so much. That’s family.” And Mariah seems proud of how far she and Nick have come since their split in 2014 and subsequent divorce."They spend time with him, and they have a good time; they spend time with me, and they have a good time," she explained to Harper's Bazaar in July 2025. "I want to make sure I’m always fair about the situation because it’s tough to grow up with divorced parents."In addition to being father to Moroccan and Monroe, Nick shares Zion Mixolydian, Zillion Heir and Beautiful Zeppelin with Abby De La Rosa; Golden “Sagon,” Powerful Queen and Rise Messiah with Brittany Bell, Legendary Love with Bre Tiesi, Onyx Ice with LaNisha Cole and Halo Marie and the late Zen with Alyssa Scott.

Of course, we have to include Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin. After all, the Oscar winner and the Coldplay singer—who share kids Apple Martin and Moses Martin—did popularize the phrase “consciously uncouple” when they announced their split in 2014.“Chris and I committed to putting them first, and that’s harder than it looks,” Gwyneth said on a 2020 episode of The Drew Barrymore Show. “Because some days, you really don't want to be with the person that you’re getting divorced from. But if you're committed to having family dinner, then you do it. And you take a deep breath, and you look the person in the eye, and you remember your pact, and you smile, and you hug, and you make a joke, and you just recommit to this new relationship that you're trying to foster.”And the Goop mogul noted she and the musician will always be family."That's how it will be forever," she continued. "Some days it's not as good as it looks. We also have good days and bad days. But I think it's driving towards the same purpose of unity and love and really what's best for them. We have this idea that just because we break up we can't love the things about the person anymore that we loved and that's not true."

After divorcing in 2022, Gisele Bündchen and Tom Brady had to tackle a new challenge. “I think there’s easier days than others,” the supermodel, who shares kids Benjamin and Vivian with the former quarterback as well as a baby with husband Joaquim Valente, admitted in a 2024 interview with ABC News’ Robin Roberts, later adding, “They’re super smart children. They know what they can get away with. So I think it’s natural that it has different rules, and then kids just adapt. And they’re going to try to do what they want. And I can only control what I do.” And as Gisele put it, it’s all about balance.“Tom has time with them, and I have time with them,” she added, “which I think is amazing because they get to really experience—again, more-enriching for their lives—two different worlds, and they get to learn from two different worlds and that’s wonderful for them I think.” Tom also shed some light on how the exes are on the same team."I'm trying to raise them—we all are, myself and their mom—in a very loving way toward one another," the athlete, who also shares son Jack with ex Bridget Moynahan, told E! News in 2023, "to be very kind, to be empathetic and to have great perspective. Our kids are growing up in different ways than we grew up but also we want to raise them with the right values."

Having played a superhero, Ben Affleck knows one when he sees one IRL. And he includes ex-wife Jennifer Garner—with whom he shares three kids—in that league."Jen is a superhero mom,” the Oscar winner—whose divorce from the 13 Going on 30 star was announced in 2015 and finalized three years later—told E! News in 2016. “She’s an amazing mother, and I'm really lucky to have her as a partner to co-parent these kids with. We try our best, we put them first and that's what we do."

While Gigi Hadid and Zayn Malik’s split in 2021 made headlines, they’ve been able to move forward together as co-parents for the sake of their daughter Khai.  “Co-parenting is good,” the One Direction alum said on a 2023 episode of Call Her Daddy. “We have a really good relationship for Khai. She’s the main importance. So yeah, it’s going well I think.” As for their advice for other parents in similar situations?“Just keeping the importance of the child’s happiness at the forefront,” Gigi told The Sunday Times that same year. “You have a long life alongside this person.” And the fact that Khai “can be with both parents,” the supermodel continued, “makes me very happy.”

Khloe Kardashian is keeping up a co-parenting relationship with ex Tristan Thompson. However, the reality star has admitted that maintaining this bond with the basketball player—who was at the center of several cheating scandals during their time together—for the sake of their children True and Tatum Thompson hasn’t always been easy. "It's way harder when you're really mad at someone, it's really hard to sit in their face in front of your kids and be like, 'Hi!'" she told tmrw in January 2024, per People, later adding, "Trust me, that's not how I feel every day. I had to learn to take control of my feelings. There were so many times that my feelings got control of me and I was impulsive and I tweeted something or posted something and things that you regret. But in my opinion, I'll never regret being a nice person."And ultimately, Khloe wants her kids to have a strong connection with Tristan, who is also dad to son Prince from his relationship with Jordan Craig and fathered son Theo with Maralee Nichols.  "I want my kids to have beautiful relationships with their dad,” the Good American mogul added. “And if we're blessed enough to have a dad that wants to be there and wants to show up and be hands-on, why would I prevent that from happening?”

While Orlando Bloom and Miranda Kerr broke up in 2013, they’re still part of a co-parenting fellowship for son Flynn.

One that includes everyone in the Lord of the Rings actor and model's family: Orlando also shares daughter Daisy Dove with ex Katy Perry, and Miranda has sons sons Hart, Myles and Pierre with husband Evan Spiegel.  "When it comes to special occasions when we have to be together, we work it out," the model told The Drew Barrymore Show in 2020. "So we have compromises that we work out together for what is the best for our whole family? But we really do always think of what is the best thing for Flynn? And I just think that that’s the most important thing at the end of the day."

Matt Bellamy, Kate Hudson & Chris Robinson

Unlike a love fern, Kate Hudson doesn’t think she has to let her amicable bond with exes Chris Robinson and Matt Bellamy die.“Chris and I just need to check in once in a while,” the How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days actress told The Sunday Times in 2022 of her former spouse and dad to son Ryder.As for Matt, dad to her son Bingham, he's "so wonderful—I couldn’t have asked for a better co-parent," she continued. "For me it’s like, you loved this person. That doesn’t just go away, but you can re-establish a different kind of love. You can have an amazing time with an ex-partner because you’re really only focused on the love of your child.”Kate is also mom to daughter Rani, whom she shares with fiancé Danny Fujikawa.“It might not look traditional from the outside, but on the inside I feel like we’re killing it,” she added. “The unit that I’ve created with three children with three different fathers is a seriously strong unit, and it’s ours.”

Sometimes, it can seem like co-parents are galaxies apart. But Anna Faris has suggested that her relationship with ex Chris Pratt, with whom she shares son Jack, and his wife Katherine Schwarzenegger has grown."We're all getting much closer, and I so appreciate that," The House Bunny  actress, who split from the Guardians of the Galaxy actor in 2017 and finalized their divorce the following year, told People in 2022. "They're very protective of me, and I want to be very protective of them. I so appreciate their support."In fact, Anna called Katherine—who also shares daughters Lyla and Eloise and son Ford with Chris—"awesome.""She's just on top of it," the Mom star continued about The Gift of Forgiveness author. "I love how she is with Jack."And ultimately, Anna—who is now married to cinematographer Michael Barrett—indicated she's happy with how things are going for the blended family."It feels just much easier now that time has passed," she told the outlet. "It feels really good to not live with that internal churning of unpleasantness."

It's good when co-parents wannabe on the same page, and Mel B admits it took a while for her and ex Eddie Murphy to form this kind of relationship.

"I think being in the kind of [situation] that I was in, it was hard for me to step out and have that relationship [with Eddie] flourish," the Spice Girls member told Us Weekly in May 2025 , while reflecting on her past struggles with PTSD and coercive control. "I managed to do it bit by bit."However, Mel B, who shares teenage Angel with Eddie, says their friendship has "flourished even more" in recent years."Angel is coming over [to Murphy’s house]," she continued. "They spend time together. They go on holiday together. He has [10] kids and he’s a proper father."

While The O.C. had plenty of drama, that doesn't mean that Rachel Bilson's co-parenting relationship with ex Hayden Christensen has to be the same way."Everything's good," the actress, who shares daughter Briar Rose with the Star Wars alum, told People in 2024. "Everything's in a really good place. She is so beautifully flourishing and has the support completely surrounding her from every side."

#799. West Ham turn to Scott Parker after sacking Nuno Espírito Santo as head coach

West Ham intent on instant return to Premier League

Nuno took over from Graham Potter in September 2025

West Ham are poised to appoint Scott Parker as manager after sacking Nuno Espírito Santo. The club have acted after a disappointing start to the Championship season and have moved for Parker, a former West Ham midfielder, in an attempt to get their push for automatic promotion back on track.

Nuno was under increasing pressure after Saturday’s 3-1 defeat by West Bromwich Albion left the favourites to win the title in eighth, four points off second-placed Swansea. West Ham kept faith with the 52-year-old Portuguese after last season’s relegation from the Premier League but recent form placed Nuno under renewed threat and led to his dismissal on Tuesday morning.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

West Ham had already identified Parker as their preferred candidate to take over. The 46-year-old has been out of work since leaving Burnley after their relegation from the Premier League last April and is expected to take over on a two-and-a-half-year deal. It is hoped that Parker, who spent four years at West Ham as a player, will be in charge for Wednesday’s trip to Cardiff.

If a deal cannot be completed in time then Mark Noble, the club’s sporting director, will oversee the match against Cardiff, with help from Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville. Noble, who is understood to have been one of several influential voices who felt Nuno’s time was up after 13 months in charge, is expected to be part of Parker’s backroom staff.

David Sullivan, then the club’s largest shareholder, wanted to sack Nuno after last season’s relegation from the Premier League. Daniel Kretinsky, the Czech billionaire, pushed for continuity. Sullivan then resigned as a joint-chair and director of West Ham to fight what he described as “false allegations” around his personal conduct. Kretinsky became West Ham’s biggest shareholder in September, buying a stake of 46%. The agreement saw Sullivan, who is not on the board, increase his stake from 38% to 40%.

Kretinsky has assumed more power and is said to have been unhappy with Nuno after attending West Ham’s 3-2 defeat by Southampton at the London Stadium. There was further disquiet in the directors’ box when West Brom handed West ham a second consecutive home defeat. Kretinsky has recognised it was a mistake to stick with Nuno, who is due £3m in compensation.

Nuno had 33 games to save West Ham from relegation after replacing Graham Potter in September 2025. But the former Nottingham Forest manager made inconsistent and baffling team selections, fell out with a host of players, made poor signings and was not popular with many non-playing staff members. Nuno has also faced internal criticism because of his reluctance to use the defensive midfielders Edson Álvarez and Soungoutou Magassa this season.

West Ham, who have two wins from their last six league games, backed Nuno in the transfer market last January. There was surprise within the recruitment department when a search for more firepower in attack saw almost £50m spent on Pablo Felipe and Taty Castellanos. Both strikers underwhelmed in the Premier League and have not found it any easier in the Championship.

While West Ham’s squad is far from perfect, the internal view is results should be better this season, especially as Nuno was able to break the EFL transfer record by spending £22m on Arne Engels from Celtic last summer. It is understood Nuno lost support in the dressing room in recent weeks. Nils Koppen, the director of recruitment, was especially unhappy with him.

The hope is that Parker, a promotion specialist, can revive West Ham. The 46-year-old has led Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham into the top flight. His managerial record in the Premier League is less impressive but West Ham’s current aim is simply to get out of the Championship. They feel that Parker is a safe pair of hands and believe his connection with West Ham means he understands the club.

Parker joined West Ham from Newcastle in 2007 and loved his time in east London. He was named the club’s player of the year on three occasions but he left for Tottenham following relegation in 2011.

#798. The referee who became a role model after bouncing back from Diaz error

We're in a goldfish bowl - England on VAR mistake

If anyone can talk about the highs and lows of being a referee, it is Darren England.

Three years ago, when acting as the video assistant referee (VAR), a blunder in a game between Tottenham and Liverpool stalled his career for months.

Luis Diaz scored for Liverpool, but his goal was flagged as offside. In a lapse of concentration, and despite the VAR image showing Diaz was onside, England said "check complete". The goal remained disallowed.

The South Yorkshire official suddenly found not only himself in the full glare of the media, but his family too.

"Refereeing is about low points and high points," England tells BBC Sport. "It's a rollercoaster of emotions.

"That was a low point. The lowest point, of course."

Today, the 40-year-old's career is revived. He is considered one of the most-trusted referees in the Premier League - both on the field and as a VAR.

Throughout 2026, England has regularly been given some of English football's biggest matches - including Manchester City's 1-0 win over Chelsea in the FA Cup final.

"So we flip it," England says, moving the conversation along to the game at Wembley. "That was a huge high for me, the pinnacle as a referee."

And on Tuesday, England has been promoted to a VAR in the Champions League for the first time, as Galatasaray take on Stuttgart.

Darren England made it to the Premier League as an assistant referee before becoming a referee, working his way back up from the National League

The game has changed immeasurably in the 11 years since England swapped his flag for a whistle.

England says referees are now "dressed like RoboCop" as they carry so much additional equipment, such as communication devices.

The biggest change has been the introduction of VAR, which had only been in the Premier League for a few months when England refereed Southampton v Wolves in January 2020.

"It's certainly not changed the way I make decisions," England insists. "If I play on on a penalty decision, some people think the perception is 'oh you're waiting for VAR to get involved'.

"No, I've played on because I don't think it's a penalty.

"But I would rather be driving home from a game now thinking, 'OK, I misread it live, I've had the opportunity to go to the screen and we've corrected it'."

England underlines this, rejecting the notion that referees "don't care about football" when they get a decision wrong.

"It couldn't be further away from the truth," he says. "It's a myth that we go home, we switch off.

"It spoils your weekend if you make a decision that's had a big impact in the game.

From the VAR audio of the Diaz incident, it was clear England and his assistant VAR, Dan Cook were immediately aware they had made a huge mistake.

But the game was only 34 minutes old. They would have to get through the next hour.

"Once I realised I'd made the error, it's a really difficult place to try to forget that and move on," England says.

"I can't just physically stand up and walk out and leave it alone. A lot of resilience was needed - a lot of experience as well."

England described how the VAR hub is a "high pressure" and sanitised environment, with "mental fatigue" taking its toll.

There is no match commentary, just the conversation of the officiating team through their headsets.

"You don't have the atmosphere of the crowd," England says. "You hear some of the crowd sometimes, but it's just a noise.

"When you've had a busy match, you're constantly checking everything. You can come out of the hub sometimes and mentally you're exhausted."

What followed was a period of intense media scrutiny which England - and his family - were not prepared for.

The story dominated newspaper headlines, radio phone-ins and social media coverage for days.

Liverpool issued a statement that said "sporting integrity" had been "undermined".

Photographers gathered outside his children's school to try to get a picture of him for the newspapers.

One story highlighted the value of his home, while family photographs were taken from his wife's Facebook account.

"The aftermath obviously was really difficult to deal with," England says. "It was challenging because it's the goldfish bowl of the Premier League.

"But when mistakes happen, then you're in the public eye and criticism's inevitably going to come your way.

"That was difficult because it affected my family as well. We had people outside my girls' school, journalists and things like that.

"That then affects you not as a referee, but as a human being."

After the Diaz mistake, England was immediately removed from selection in the Premier League and began a process of rehabilitation.

It would be almost three months before he refereed a top-flight game again, and he did not return to full rotation until February.

It was a longer road back to the VAR room - six-and-a-half months before he was the video official in the Premier League again.

He was eased back in by the Football Association and given a couple of FA Cup ties with Michael Oliver alongside him as the support VAR.

"I did a lot of work with a sports psychologist," England says. "The support, not just from Pro Ref but more importantly family and friends, was really crucial.

"It's about perspective as well. There's a danger that we can think we're saving lives at times, but we also realise how important it is.

"I remained as focused as I could be, working hard, trusting myself, because for all that decision in the Liverpool-Tottenham game, I've made hundreds of other decisions that are correct."

All that focus has paid off, with England the VAR for a decision which was dubbed the 'biggest VAR call ever' as West Ham had a stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal disallowed on review in May.

England said he "absolutely understood the magnitude" of that decision but "kept calm" under pressure.

Six days later, England took charge of the FA Cup final.

"We're quick to always focus on mistakes and the low points, and how we deal with that," England adds.

"It's one of the targets when you start becoming professional that you want to referee the FA Cup final.

"You only do it once and it's a real honour."

VAR has added a huge amount of additional scrutiny on officials, not just from the press.

England says he will get quizzed by parents on the school run about decisions over the weekend - and not just his own. And then there are the fans online.

"If you want to go searching for good feedback on social media and you're listening to phone-ins, you probably won't find much," England says.

"That can have an impact on how you perform on the field.

"I don't have social media, I made a decision not to. But other people have different preferences and I respect that as well.

"But you have to manage your time accordingly, to be aware that you can never really switch off from football."

To dive or not to dive? Football's big dilemma

Wenger's 'daylight' offside trial unlikely to be extended

Is a double drop from Premier League becoming more common?

England's rise from his "lowest" point has been confirmed by his refereeing appointments.

But it has also been made clear by the respect of his colleagues - which BBC Sport saw first-hand at a referees' training camp at Loughborough University.

Hugh Dallas, the Professional Referee Group director, was at the front of the room, preparing to lead a discussion about decisions from the previous weekend. He paused for a moment, then beckoned forward a referee who, he said, had "become a role model".

That was England, who had recently taken charge of his 100th top-flight game. He was greeted with warm applause as he was handed a Premier League presentation box containing a plaque and a medal.

It is a journey that has taken England from his first match in the village of Royston, five miles outside Barnsley, to the top of the game - twice.

England, who qualified as a referee aged 15, is one of a few to come from inside the game, alongside the likes of Farai Hallam and Sam Allison.

He was working at Barnsley's academy, coaching during training in the week and matches on a Sunday, while refereeing on a Saturday.

Eventually, he had to choose between the two as a professional career - refereeing won.

England first made it to the Premier League as an assistant. Then, in 2015 at the age of 28, he decided to start again in the National League as a referee and work back up.

Within four and a half years, he would take charge of his first Premier League fixture.

"I had the chance of potentially going to tournaments (as an assistant), or do I back myself as a referee?" England says. "Thankfully, it paid off."

Referees should only get the chance to referee the FA Cup final once - the two exceptions since 1901 being Anthony Taylor and Michael Oliver, who took charge of the match twice in recent seasons

England's progress has been closely monitored by Uefa, which has moved him through the levels as a VAR.

After 10 Conference League appointments, and six in the Europa League, this week he is elevated to the Champions League.

"We work extremely hard, and we continue to work extremely hard to stay at that level," England adds.

"Players in the Premier League, they're getting better and better. So we have to keep on improving as well."

After the honour of taking charge of the FA Cup final, does England have any other goals in his career on the field?

"When I don't have targets, that's probably time to come off the field," he says.

"I want to do all the finals that we can do. So obviously, the Carabao Cup, the Championship play-off final.

Three years ago, refereeing an FA Cup final and being a VAR in the Champions League seemed a world away for England.

Now, he's earned the right to have those targets.

#797. Marathoner Dies of Rhabdomyolysis: What to Know About Rare Condition

Rhabdomyolysis, which caused the death of NYC marathoner Rachel Apa on Nov. 1, is a relatively rare condition, but here's what to know about what it is, who's at risk and how it becomes fatal.

When you think about athletes, you tend to think about stamina, strength and being in peak physical condition.

But anyone pushing his or her body to its limits also has to beware of overdoing it. The tragic death of Rachel Apa, a former college athlete who collapsed two miles from the finish line of the New York City Marathon, is an extreme case of a body fatally breaking down within a few hours, but a reminder that it can happen.

According to her father Steve Apa, Rachel died of rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which damaged muscle tissue breaks down and sends harmful proteins into the bloodstream.

“It’s unfathomable,” he told the New York Times. “Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old.”

Rachel, running her first marathon, had texted her dad after passing the 9-mile mark of the 26.2-mile route, which starts on Staten Island and finishes in Central Park, "I feel amazing. I've never felt this good."

Steve texted back from the family's home in Lewisberry, Penn., per NBC News, "Great, don’t overdo it. First marathon. This is a learning run. Don’t overdo it.”

Rachel had played field hockey for Bucknell University, was a regular exerciser and had trained for months ahead of the event.

“She was always on the go, always go," Steve said, "and it doesn’t matter if it’s school or sports or whatever it is. She was go."

So, how the heck does something like this happen?

Here is what to know about rhabdomyolysis, who is most at risk and more:

If you had never heard of rhabdomyolysis (or "rhabdo," as it's often abbreviated) you're hardly alone, as it's considered relatively rare, with about 26,000 cases reported in the United States each year, meaning it affects .0076 percent of the country's population.

According to the National Institutes of Health, rhabdomyolysis is a condition in which skeletal muscles break down and release intracellular components such as myoglobin, creatine phosphokinase (CPK), electrolytes and sarcoplasmic proteins into the bloodstream.

When toxic components of your muscle fibers enter your circulation system and kidneys, it can lead to acute kidney injury (AKI), electrolyte disturbances, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (a blood clotting disorder), per the NIH.

A "crushing injury" is the most common cause of rhabdomyolysis, according to the Cleveland Clinic, while overexertion (too much exercise without rest) and severe dehydration and overheating can also cause rapid muscle breakdown.

Cited causes of rhabdomyolysis also include certain medications, such as antipsychotic, antidepressant and antiviral medications, as well as statins; long periods of inactivity and physical conditions such as muscular dystrophy.

Endurance athletes and members of the military—i.e. those who engage in high-intensity physical activity—are considered more at risk, per the Cleveland Clinic, as are firefighters and others who work in hot environments and people over 65, as they're considered more prone to falls that could lead to injuries and prolonged immobility.

“Exertional rhabdomyolysis can occur after strenuous exercise and from high-intensity workouts during which the muscles are overused,” Niloofar Nobakht, MD, associate clinical professor of nephrology, told UCLA Health in 2023. “You can also get rhabdo from direct trauma, such as a crushing injury from a motor vehicle accident or a fall.”

But almost any intense activity can cause rhabdo, most commonly among people who are trying something new, according to Eric Rawson, chair of the department of health, nutrition and exercise science at Messiah College in Pennsylvania.

"You can be fit, and I can come up with a workout that you are unaccustomed to, and that could be what causes rhabdo," he told the NY Times in 2017, explaining why it's so important to start out at a beginner's level of a new activity before notching up the intensity.

Experiencing sore or weak muscles a few days after exercising, muscle swelling and abnormally dark or otherwise off-color urine can be signs of the condition.

The Cleveland Clinic notes that symptoms usually develop one to three days after a muscle injury, and persistent soreness doesn't always register as a potential life-threatening complication.

Rhabdomyolysis is survivable but requires prompt treatment, according to medical experts. Usually the condition is treated with fluids and electrolytes administered intravenously, while extreme kidney damage could require dialysis.

“We might start with an IV fluid and closely monitor electrolytes such as potassium, phosphorus and calcium," UCLA's Nobakht said. "Potassium and calcium are the two main electrolytes that play a significant role in recovering muscle function."

Witnesses said that Rachel Apa collapsed around the 24-mile mark of the New York City Marathon in Central Park. Three people, two of whom said they were doctors, took turns administering CPR, spectator Michaela Nicholas told the NY Times. New York Road Runners, which organizes the marathon, said event medical staff used a defibrillator on the fallen athlete before paramedics arrived and transported her to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead after six hours of attempted life-saving measures.

University of Michigan Health emergency medicine physician Dr. Bradley Uren told the publication that, for Rachel, "that worst case scenario happened just very, very quickly."

#796. McTominay returns as Penrice earns first Scotland call

Scott McTominay missed games for club and country in September and October following a minor heart procedure

Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney and Che Adams return to the Scotland squad for the remaining Nations League matches at home to North Macedonia and away to Switzerland.

There is a first call up for James Penrice and uncapped Kristi Montgomery, a late addition last time, retains his place.

Scott McKenna and Kenny McLean miss out through injury, while Lennon Miller, Josh Doig, Colby Donovan and James Wilson drop out.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli chose an extended pool of 28 for the first four matches, which included disappointing home defeats to Switzerland and Slovenia.

For these fixtures, the Belgian has gone with 26, sticking with four goalkeepers.

Scotland are third in Group B1 and require a minimum of four points to have any chance of finishing second to feature in the promotion play-offs.

One point would stave off any threat of relegation.

Switzerland lead the way on maximum points, with Slovenia three ahead of Scotland.

Left-back Penrice, 27, has impressed with Rangers since arriving on loan from AEK Athens, while Blackburn Rovers midfielder Montgomery, 22, has started all but one Championship match this season.

Napoli star McTominay has scored four goals in seven outings since recovering from a minor heart procedure.

Adams has doubled his Torino tally for the term with two goals in five Serie A games after a brief lay off with an adductor issue.

Captain Andy Robertson will surpass Sir Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps should the Tottenham full-back feature in both matches on 13 and 16 November.

#795. ESPN's Michael Wilbon Announces Indefinite Leave Amid Health Issues

Pardon the Interruption cohost Michael Wilbon announced that he will be taking a leave of absence from ESPN and ABC amid multiple ongoing health issues: "This isn't retirement."

The longtime ESPN commentator and cohost of Pardon the Interruption with Tony Kornheiser announced he will be taking an indefinite leave of absence from the network and ABC amid multiple health struggles.

“This isn't retirement, but it is a trip to the injured list. Hopefully not an extended one,” Wilbon posted on X Nov. 2. “Struggles with multiple health issues in recent months lead me to take an indefinite leave of absence from my PTI and NBA duties at ESPN and ABC.”

“Probably, I should have listened to medical professionals and people closest to me,” he admitted, “yep Kornheiser included, who saw worrisome signs in recent years that suggested I take time away earlier. But I didn’t.”

While he didn’t go into details about the struggles, the 67-year-old did assure his fans that it was not related to alcohol or gambling.

He also expressed his gratitude to his colleagues for encouraging him to take time away “to concentrate on me” and keep his focus on his wellbeing.

“I have no idea exactly how this part of my journey will wind up,” Wilbon wrote. “The goal is to come out of it feeling much better than I do now and ready to return to sparring with Tony.”

Wilbon—who began hosting Pardon the Interruption in 2001—shed more insight on his health on the Nov. 2 episode of Kornheiser’s podcast The Tony Kornheiser Show, sharing that he was diagnosed with diabetes in 2008 and the condition is “part of what I have to deal with right now,” although it’s not the only issue.

“For people who pay attention, I’ve been away,” he said. “I didn’t do the show for a week last week. I didn’t do the show for a week because I was just exhausted. Beyond exhausted, lifeless.”

Wilbon confessed “this had been going on for a while,” with those closest to him trying to get him to take time off.

“But that’s not my way. My way is to run through the brick wall, go to work. You go to work. That’s what you do,” he said. “You go to work until somebody stops you from going to work.”

“Well, that’s what this is now,” he told Kornheiser. “And so I probably shouldn’t have gone to work for a week. I know you wanted me to take some time off. That was the right move.”

For more celebs who have faced their own health struggles, keep reading.

The Jessie alum opened up about her "hellish" migraines, sharing how they've worsened after suffering five concussions over the course of her life.

Now, the former Disney Channel star needs to close her eyes to "think better."

And right now, I can’t do a squat on my foot. I can’t do a one legged squat, I fall. It’s like I had a stroke or something.”

The Kim Possible alum continued, "Unfortunately a fragment got lodged behind my eye and it is too risky to remove surgically at this time. Doctors will continue to monitor me (I can see normally at the moment)."

The actress said she was grateful to be alive. "I love my daughters, husband, family, and friends so much," she said. "I saw my life flash before my eyes and I’m telling you, hug the people around you every chance you can. Life can change in an instant."

While the internet isn't always a kind place, Amy Schumer is happy that, in this case, it helped her get answers."The internet really came for me after doing a bunch of press, and I was like, 'OK everybody, relax,'" Amy recalled of her "puffier" face on a January 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy. "But then doctors were chiming in in the comments and they were like, 'No no, we think something’s really up. Your face looks so crazy that we think something’s up. And I’m like, ‘Wait, I’m getting trolled by doctors?’"After these doctors said they thought she had Cushing syndrome and that it may be caused by spiking coritsol levels or steroid injections, the Life & Beth creator thought, "Wait, I have been getting steroid injections in my scars.""I had a breast reduction, a C-section, whatever, and so I was getting these steroid injections," Amy said. "So it gave me this thing called Cushing syndrome, which I wouldn’t have known if the internet hadn’t come for me so hard."Toda, Amy is just relieved she's OK. As she shared in a February 2024 News Not Noise newsletter, "Finding out I have the kind of Cushing that will just work itself out and I'm healthy was the greatest news imaginable."

Casey Fitzgerald's Neck Injury From Hockey Skate Blade

The AHL player was cut by a fellow player's skate during a game in December 2024 and received 25 stitches. His father, New Jersey Devils general manager Tom Fitzgerald later told ESPN after his son was fully recovered, "We're very lucky. I don't wish that on any parent."

Hailey Bieber had the "scariest moment" of her life when she was having breakfast with husband Justin Bieber and started experiencing stroke-like symptoms in March 2022."Justin was like, 'Are you OK?'" the Rhode skincare mogul shared a month later on YouTube, "and I just didn't respond because I wasn't sure. And then he asked me again and when I went to respond, I couldn't speak. The right side of my face started drooping. I couldn't get a sentence out."While Hailey said the facial drooping stopped and her speech came back, she went to the hospital to make sure she was OK."They did some scans and they were able to see that I had suffered a small blood clot to my brain," the model added, "which they labeled and categorized as something called a TIA [Transient Ischemic Attack]."Later, Hailey went to the University of California, Los Angeles, where she found out she had a hole in her heart called a patent foramen ovale (PFO).She explained the blood clot had traveled into her heart, "escaped" through the hole and went to her brain, leading to the TIA.Hailey said she had a successful PFO closure procedure and was now feeling great.

The same year Hailey had her health scare, Justin experienced one of his own.In June 2022, the "Baby" singer shared he was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a condition that caused temporary paralysis to parts of his face and forced him to cancel the remainder of his Justice World Tour."It is from this virus that attacks the nerve in my ear and my facial nerves and has caused my face to have paralysis," Justin explained in an Instagram video at the time. "As you can see, this eye is not blinking. I can't smile on this side of my face. This nostril will not move. So, there's full paralysis on this side of my face."In fact, he told his followers it had gotten "progressively harder to eat." But after a while, the paralysis went away."He's doing really well," Hailey said on a June 2022 episode of Good Morning America, later adding, "He's feeling a lot better. Obviously, it was just a very scary and random situation to happen, but he's going to be totally OK and I'm just grateful that he's fine."

While Jamie Foxx initially kept details of his April 2023 hospitalization private, he later opened up about what he went through.One day in Atlanta, "I was having such a bad headache, so I asked my boy, I said, ‘Listen, I need an aspirin,’” the Oscar winner said in his 2024 Netflix special What Had Happened Was... “Before I could get the Aspirin, I went out. I don’t remember 20 days.”Jamie said he was initially taken to a doctor who gave him a cortisone shot and then sent him home. However, his concerned sister Deidra Dixon then drove him to a hospital, where they got an answer: He had a brain bleed that led to a stroke.Twenty days after undergoing an operation, the Django Unchained woke up May 4 in a wheelchair and couldn’t walk. He then went to Chicago for rehabilitation and therapy."All I can tell you is that I appreciate every prayer,” he said, “because I needed every prayer.”

Tracey Yukich's Medical Emergency on The Biggest Loser

The reality star revealed that she "died" while running a mile during the first challenge of the NBC competition series.

“I don't remember a lot,” she explained on Fit for TV: The Reality of The Biggest Loser. “I remember hearing the helicopter. I just felt like I was floating. And then my grandpa was there. And then I saw darkness. But then I saw light. So I knew, I knew I died that day.”

“My organs were literally shutting down,” she continued. “I didn't realize that I had rhabdomyolysis. And rhabdomyolysis is your body's way of saying, ‘I'm going to shut down on you.’”

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. "I’d had an aneurysm, an arterial rupture."Emilia had immediate surgery to seal the aneurysm, calling the pain "unbearable." While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "Everybody just came to my rescue."Because of other medical concerns, Cori ended up staying in the hospital longer than she initially expected."I could have went home after my stroke, but my lupus wasn't doing so well," the Snoop's Fatherhood: Cori and Wayne's Story star continued. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

#793. Andoni Iraola calls on Liverpool to sharpen up in attack before Fenerbahce test

Reds target fourth straight Champions League win

Turkish side led by ex-Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt

Andoni Iraola has said Liverpool must improve their attacking play but dismissed concerns over the contrast between his team’s output in the Premier League and Champions League.

Liverpool boast a 100% record in Europe this season and can take a significant step towards qualification for the knockout phase with victory away at Fenerbahce on Wednesday.

Iraola’s side failed to register a shot on target, according to Opta, during Sunday’s defeat by Arsenal, the first time Liverpool have drawn a blank in a Premier League home game since their records began in 2003-04. The Liverpool head coach believes the statistic did not reflect his team’s performance but admitted there is room for improvement.

“It is difficult when you lose but honestly I am happy with a lot of things from the other day,” said Iraola, who is without the injured Ryan Gravenberch in Istanbul. “But we still need to improve, especially attacking the box. A lot of times we were there with the numbers but we were not making the proper runs and waiting for second balls. We put Arsenal under pressure and they defended well but I liked a lot of things.”

Liverpool have scored more goals in three Champions League games this season (12) than in nine Premier League fixtures (11) but Iraola denied the disparity is a serious concern.

He added: “We have had better results in the Champions League and Carabao Cup than the Premier League but it’s very early in the season for these comparisons. We want to continue this run in the Champions League. This is a good chance to get to 12 points and try to qualify, and then try to finish in the top eight, but Champions League away games are difficult, especially in this stadium and this atmosphere. We have to be mentally very ready.”

Former Liverpool favourite Dirk Kuyt is poised to take charge of his first European game with the Turkish club, having replaced Ismail Kartal on an interim basis last week, although Fenerbahce announced on Tuesday night that Emre Belozoglu, the former Newcastle player, is to take over permanently.

Kuyt returned to Fenerbahce as Kartal’s assistant only this summer – he played for the club for three seasons after leaving Liverpool in 2012 – but was appointed interim coach following Kartal’s resignation in the wake of last week’s 2-1 defeat by Galatasaray.

The former Liverpool striker said: “Tomorrow will be a very special occasion for me but, at the stage we are in, I’m not the important person. It’s about the club. Romelu [Lukaku] was speaking about how important it is to show the fans – who deserve much more – a reaction and a good performance. We have really good players but we need to show up. Liverpool are an amazing team but so are Fenerbahce. If the fans show up, I think Europe will see how big this fanbase is.”

#792. Terry Dubrow Reveals Cadaveric Fat Transfers Are a "Hot New" Procedure

Terry Dubrow revealed a shocking truth, stunning Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg during his appearance on her podcast when he revealed fat transfers from cadavers are a new cosmetic trend.

Warning: You won’t be able to unlearn the knowledge Terry Dubrow recently dropped.

And, well, his intel about how plastic surgery and cadavers are connected cuts pretty deep.

But if you’re still reading this, fine. We’ll allow the Botched star himself to explain.

“The new thing is cadaveric fat transfer,” Dubrow informed Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg on the Nov. 3 episode of her eponymous podcast. “Have you heard of this?”

In response, an aghast McCarthy Wahlberg asked, “Does that mean from cadavers?”

“Yes,” Dubrow affirmed, sparking the Two and a Half Men alum to make a disgusted noise, before he added, “That’s the hot new thing.”

For the particularly macabre, here’s how it works. AlloClae, the name brand for such an injectable, is a non-surgical body contouring solution made from donated human fat tissue (yes, we’re talking about cadavers). The injectable is comprised of non-living fat cells, extracellular matrix, triglycerides and connective tissues.

The way alloClae is processed, per its website, preserves the natural 3D structure of fat cells, allowing for immediate volume without the downtime and invasiveness that comes with surgery.

For those whose minds are still reeling with concerns, Dubrow told McCarthy Wahlberg, “It's been processed and radiated and stuff like that. But there's different kinds of cadaver fat. One of the kinds, there's no cells in it. It's just the matrix and you injected it and your own fat grows into it.”

The 68-year-old emphasized, “That's the hot thing right now.”

Of course, while the trend might be new in the world of plastic surgery, the use of cadavers has been a regular practice in dentistry. Allograft bone is processed, sterilized bone harvested from deceased donors and is used in procedures such as dental bone grating, socket and ridge preservation as well as periodontal defect repair.

Though cadaveric fat transfer was a new one for McCarthy Wahlberg, allograft bone is a concept she’s previously sunk her teeth into—literally.

“Do you know how many dead bodies are in my mouth from all of my mouth surgeries that I've had?” the 54-year-old said to Dubrow. “Like, I've eaten more cadavers in the last two years than I ever thought I would.”

Nevertheless, she added, “I don't think I want cadaver's fat.”

But while cadaveric fat transfers are relatively fresh out the box, so to speak, plastic surgery itself has long existed within Hollywood. Read on for what some of your favorite celebrities have said about their cosmetic procedures—and how much they paid for them.

The Talk alum has never shied away from discussing her plastic surgeries."I’ve had a string of cosmetic procedures beginning with a browlift and facelift," she told The Telegraph in December 2023. "I had liposuction on my neck and had it lifted, too. I had my breasts lifted, my arms lipo-ed and my tummy tucked."Additionally, "I had my bum lifted and implants inserted," Osbourne continued. "Then I had a facelift three-and-a-half years ago. I was left with one eye higher than the other. It took a year to put it all right."As for how much this all cost?"Well, I haven’t kept a running total," Mrs. O admitted, "but it must top more than a million."

The Jennifer's Body actress has also been open about the changes she's made to her body, including a nose job, boob jobs, Botox and filler. And while she hasn't revealed the price tag for all her procedures, she has given a dollar-amount for her breast augmentations."My mom said that I used to go into the bathroom, and stand on the toilet, and pull up my shirt to see if my boobies had grown, and I would get really upset that I didn't have big boobs," Fox said on Alex Cooper's Call Her Daddy podcast in March 2025. "Thirty thousand dollars later, now I do."

Want to know right now (na na na) what the singer paid for the hair transplant he got in Turkey?"For what I did, it would've cost me $50,000 in America," he said on The Bootleg Kev Podcast in October 2022. "I paid, like, $7,800-$7,500."But then, Akon ended up shaving his head."I did the transplant to grow hair. The problem was my hair wasn't going," he noted on the podcast in April 2025. "So, I said, 'F--k it. I'm just going to keep it cut to keep it even.' But I actually like it better this way."

The comedian is taking those laughs all the way from the bank, revealing the hefty cost of her third facelift."It was not cheap," she noted on Josh Peck and Ben Soffer's Good Guys podcast in November 2025. "You ready? $218,000."

The price of the Dance Moms alum's veneers could be considered near the top of the pyramid."Most expensive thing I'm wearing? My teeth," she told BuzzFeed at the GLAAD Media Awards in March 2024. "These motherf--kers cost me $50,000."

Because The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star is all about the receipts, proof, timeline and screenshots, she's given a detailed account of the plastic surgery and cosmetic work she's had done.And while Gay gets a lot of it for free as the owner of a medical spa, she's still racked up a grand total."Counting all of the things I’ve had done, I’m probably $200,000 into my physical appearance," she told Bustle in November 2025 about her list, including Botox, filler, two nose jobs, blepharoplasty and $30,000 veneers, "and it was worth every penny."

Confessing the price did give her pause, the talk show host's view on her lower deep plane facelift has been nothing but positive."Why do I look like this? $90,000," she told People in July 2026. "I was worried about the cost. I don’t like to waste money. And I would never spend that on a car."

The Soup alum is ladling up an estimate for a hair transplant—one of the many he's been open about undergoing."Ten thousand dollars," he said on Mark Normand and Sam Morril's We Might Be Drunk podcast in July 2025. "It might've gone up."And McHale would know as he shared he's gotten the procedure more than once for maintenance. "I'm fully bald," he stated. "This is four transplants."
